en: Śrīḥ!
The Bhojaprabandha: The narrative of the illustrious Great King of Kings, Bhojarāja, is now told.

In the beginning, a king named Sindhula protected his subjects for a long time in the kingdom of Dhārā. When he reached old age, a son named Bhoja was born to him. When the boy was five years old, the father, perceiving his own senility and observing his younger brother Muñja—who was possessed of great strength—and seeing that his son was still a child, reflected: "If I were to bestow the kingdom upon my son while bypassing my own brother, who is capable of bearing the burden of royal fortune, it would lead to public scandal."

Alternatively, out of greed for the kingdom, Muñja might kill my young son with poison; in that case, even a bestowed kingdom would be in vain. It would result in the loss of a son and the extinction of the lineage.
Greed is the foundation of sin, and greed alone is its progenitor.
Greed gives rise to hatred, anger, and the like; greed is the cause of evil. (1)
From greed arises anger; from anger proceeds malice.
Through malice, even a wise man learned in the scriptures goes to hell.
Overcome by greed, a man may kill his mother, father, son, brother, or dearest friend, or even his own master or uterine sibling.

Having reflected thus, he gave the kingdom to Muñja and placed his son Bhoja in his lap. Then, when the king had gradually departed for heaven, Muñja—having attained the fullness of royal power—removed the chief minister named Buddhisāgara from his office by means of a seal of dismissal and appointed another in his place. Thereafter, he had the prince instructed by his teachers.

Then, in due course, a Brahmin who had mastered the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) and possessed proficiency in all branches of knowledge arrived at the assembly hall. Having approached the king and said, "May there be well-being (*svasti*)," he sat down. He said: "O King, this world calls me 'omniscient' (*sarvajña*). Therefore, ask whatever you wish.
Knowledge that resides in the throat should always be made manifest by the wise;
but that knowledge which remains with the teacher or in a book—by that, the fool is deceived. (Verse 4)

Thus he spoke to the king. Then the king, hearing those words which were rendered marvelous by the seal of the Brahmin’s self-assurance, said: “If you speak of everything that has been done and performed by me from the time of my birth until this very moment, then you are indeed omniscient. Thereupon the Brahmin recounted everything that the king had done, including even his secret deeds. Then the king, having recognized all the signs of proof, was deeply gratified.
Again, having gone five or six steps, he fell at his feet; and having seated him upon a lion-throne inlaid with sapphire, ruby, emerald, and beryl, the king said:
"Like a mother she protects, like a father she enjoins what is beneficial, and like a beloved wife she delights one, removing all weariness."
It spreads stainless fame in all directions; what prosperity does this knowledge not accomplish, like a wish-fulfilling creeper? ||5||
Then he gave ten thoroughbred horses to the best of Brahmins.

Thereupon, sitting in the assembly hall, Buddhisāgara said to the king, "O Lord, ask the Brahmin for Bhoja’s birth horoscope. Then Muñja said, "Prepare the birth horoscope for Bhoja. Then that Brahmin replied, "Bhoja must be brought to the schoolroom. Muñja, out of curiosity, had Bhoja—who was then adorning the schoolroom—brought there by his guards.

Then, having bowed with humility to the king as if he were his own father, he stood before him. Thereupon, while the circle of princes was infatuated by his beauty and grace, the astrologer, having observed Bhoja—who was like Mahendra descended upon the earth with abundant good fortune, like the god of love incarnate, and like auspiciousness personified—spoke to the king: "O King, even Viriñci is not capable of describing the rise of Bhoja’s fortune; what am I, a mere belly-filling brahmin?"

Nevertheless, I shall say something according to my own understanding: "Send Bhoja from here to the hall of study. Then, by the king's command, when Bhoja had indeed gone to the hall of study, the Brahmin said:
"For fifty-five years, seven months, and three days, the southern region along with Gauḍa must be enjoyed by King Bhoja. (6)

Thus it was said. Having heard those words, King Sumukha, as if mocking him out of cleverness, became pale-faced. Then the king, having sent the Brahmin away, went to his bed at midnight and reflected alone: "If the fortune of sovereignty goes to the prince Bhoja, then I am dead even while living.
Those very senses remain unimpaired, that same name remains, that same intellect is unobstructed, and that same speech remains."
Deprived of the warmth of wealth, that very same person becomes someone else in an instant— how strange this is!
Furthermore:
For one who is independent of the body, diligent, resolute,
and has commenced his task with intelligence, nothing whatsoever is difficult to accomplish.
Even when previous efforts and exertions have been thwarted by malice,
prosperity is nevertheless seized by the agents through the assistance of friends and ministers.
In that regard, what is difficult to achieve through effort?
Prosperities depart far away from those who are excessively full of courtesy, who are suspicious at every step, and who are fearful of reproaching others. (10)
Furthermore:
"Time drinks up the prosperity of that which is to be received, that which is to be given, and that action which ought to be done, if it is not performed quickly. (11)
Placing dishonor before him and casting pride behind his back, a wise man should secure his own interest; for the loss of one's own interest is indeed folly.
A wise person should not destroy a great deal for the sake of a small thing; this alone is true wisdom: that one protects the great by means of the small. (13)
He who does not pacify an enemy or a disease as soon as they arise will, despite possessing well-nourished limbs, be destroyed by them later on. (14)
What can enemies do, even when united, against one whose body is protected by wisdom?
They are like torrents of rain against one who holds a parasol over his head. (15)
A wise person should not undertake actions that are fruitless, those whose end is miserable, those where the gain and loss are equal, or those things which are impossible to accomplish. (16)

Then, reflecting thus, even before having eaten, during the third watch of the day, he summoned his own bodyguard and dispatched him alone to call for Vatsarāja, the mighty lord of Vaṅga. That bodyguard approached Vatsarāja and said, "The king summons you. Thereupon, having mounted his chariot and surrounded by his retinue, he arrived; alighting from the chariot, he beheld the king, prostrated himself, and sat down.
The king, having cleared the palace of all people, spoke to Vatsarāja:
“Even when pleased, a king bestows mere honor upon his servants; yet they, being thus honored, serve him even at the cost of their own lives. (17)

"Therefore, you must slay the Bhoja in the forest of Bhuvaneśvarī during the first watch of the night, and his head must be brought to the city at the end. He rose, bowed to the king, and said: "The command of Your Majesty is authoritative. Nevertheless, because of your affection for me, I wish to say something. Therefore, let my words be forgiven until the next day. O Lord, the Bhoja possesses neither wealth nor an army, nor a powerful retinue; he stands today like a ship [adrift]. How, then, is he to be slain? (18)
"O bull among kings, his devotion to your feet is as if hereditary; he is merely a burden upon his own belly. I see no cause whatsoever for his slaughter. (19)
Then the king related everything that had occurred in the assembly the following morning. Having heard this, he said with a laugh:
"Rāma is the lord of the three worlds, and Vasiṣṭha is the son of Brahmā;
by him, indeed, the auspicious hour for the royal consecration was declared. (20)
In that very moment, Rāma too was led away from the earth to the forest;
Sītā’s abduction occurred, and even the word of Brahmā became futile.
"O best of kings, who is this person born who knows so little and cares only for his own belly, that by his word you wish to kill the prince, who possesses the form of the God of Love? (22)
Furthermore: "What indeed would happen to me by doing this? What indeed would happen to me by not doing it?
Having reflected thus with his mind, a wise person should either act or not act. (23)
Whether performing what is appropriate or inappropriate, a wise person must diligently consider the final consequence of a multitude of actions.
For the ripening of deeds performed with excessive haste becomes like a piercing thorn, burning the heart until their completion. 24.
Furthermore:
"How can the minds of even the wicked turn away from one with whom they have dwelt, eaten, laughed, and conversed in private with full confidence—until death? (25)

Furthermore—once this man is slain, the great ministers, who are the objects of the supreme affection of the aged King Sindhula and remain loyal only to your will, will submerge your city like clouds with surging waves. Although you have long since established deep roots, the citizens generally regard Bhoja as the lord of the earth.
Moreover—
Even when good deeds have been performed, bad policy surely robs one of fortune;
for a swarm of wind-blown insects extinguishes the flame of a lamp that has been constantly fed with oil. (26)

"Your Majesty, the killing of one's own son is never for one's benefit. Having heard these words of Vatsarāja, the king became enraged and said: "You alone are the sovereign of the kingdom, not a mere servant!
He who does not strive when commanded by his master is a wretched servant;
even his life is as useless as the teat of a goat without a kid. (27)
Thus he spoke. Then the King of Vatsa, thinking, "One must consider what is appropriate for the occasion," remained silent.

Now, as the sun was sinking low, the members of the assembly—seeing the King of Vatsa descending from the terrace of his lofty palace like an enraged God of Death—became terrified and departed for their own homes under various pretexts. Thereupon, having dispatched his own servants to protect his residence and having directed his chariot toward the palace of Bhuvaneśvarī, the King of Vatsa sent a messenger to summon the Bhoja prince and his preceptor.

He said to the Paṇḍita, “Father, the King of Vatsa summons you. Upon hearing this, the Paṇḍita—like one struck by a thunderbolt, like one possessed by a spirit, or like one seized by a demon—was led away by that servant, who took him by the hand. Then the wise King of Vatsa, having saluted him, said: “Paṇḍita, father, sit down. Bring Prince Jayanta from the schoolroom. Having asked the approaching Prince Jayanta about whatever he had studied, he brought him in.

Again he said to the scholar, "Brahmin, bring the prince of Bhoja. Then Bhoja, having learned what had transpired, approached in a rage, his eyes blazing as if on fire with blood, and said, "Ah, you wretch! What power do you have to bring me—the king's chief prince—out of the royal palace all alone? Having said this, Bhoja seized the slipper from the left foot and struck the King of Vatsa in the region of the palate.

Then Vatsarāja said, "Bhoja, we are executors of the king’s command. Having placed the boy in the chariot and unsheathed his sword, he departed quickly for the abode of Mahāmāyā. When Bhoja was thus seized, the people raised a great clamor and a tumultuous outcry began. Crying out "What? What?", the guards arrived shouting; learning that Bhoja had been taken away for execution, they rushed into the elephant stables, the camel pens, the horse stables, and the chariot sheds, slaughtering everyone there.

Then, in the main streets, on the ramparts and platforms of the royal palace, on the outer parapets, and in the vicinity of the city, the sky was filled with the tumultuous roar of kettledrums, tabors, clay drums, hand-drums, and gongs.

Some, by means of a stainless sword; some by poison; some by a spear; some by a noose; some by fire; some by an axe; some by a crescent-headed arrow; some by a lance; some by a javelin; and some by water—in the very stream—Brāhmaṇa women, princes, royal servants, kings, and citizens gave up their lives.

Then Sāvitrī, the mother of the Bhoja king—who stood like the Mother of the Universe—heard from the mouth of a maidservant about the condition of her son. Covering her eyes with both hands and weeping, she said: "My son, what state have you been brought to by your paternal uncle? Those vows and fasts which I observed for your sake have today become fruitless for me. All ten directions appear empty. My son, the fortunes of the All-Knowing and All-Powerful God have been swept away!
My son, look at this group of maidservants whose heads have been suddenly severed! Having said this, she fell to the ground.

Then, when the fire had blazed up and the sky was darkened by the mass of rising smoke, and while the orb of the sun had sunk into the western ocean as if out of fear of sin, the King of Vatsa approached the palace of Mahāmāyā and said to Bhoja: "O Prince, deity of your servants! A certain Brahmin, an expert in the science of astrology, has prophesied your attainment of the kingdom; consequently, the King has ordered your execution. Bhoja replied:
"The exile of Rāma, the subjugation of Bali, and the forest-dwelling of the sons of Pāṇḍu—"
Reflecting upon the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis, King Nala’s fall from his kingdom, and Rāvaṇa’s confinement in prison—all men perish by the power of Time; who indeed can protect them? (28)
The son of the ocean of nectar, born together with Lakṣmī, the Kaustubha gem, and the Pārijāta tree, was borne upon his head by Lord Śambhu as a mark of affectionate favor;
yet even today the Moon does not abandon the blemish ordained by fate.
By whom else can the course of destiny be transgressed, which is like a mere line etched in stone?
Wandering over rugged lands, climbing mountains, crossing the ocean, being bound in fetters, and entering caves—how indeed can such a ripening of destiny be overcome? (30)

By his will, the ocean becomes dry land and dry land becomes the ocean; a speck of dust becomes Mount Meru and Mount Meru becomes a bedbug; grass becomes a thunderbolt and the thunderbolt becomes as common as grass;
fire becomes cool and ice becomes fire.
Salutation to that God, who is devoted to the wonderful addiction of playful pastimes. || 31 ||

Then, taking a leaf from a *vaṭa* tree and folding it into a pouch, he cut his calf with a knife and placed the blood into that pouch. Having written a certain verse on one leaf with grass, he said to the calf: "Noble one, this leaf must be given to the king; you too must carry out the king's command. Then, at the time of Bhoja’s abandonment of life, Vatsarāja’s younger brother, observing the splendor of his radiant face, said: "Dharma alone is a true friend who follows one even unto death."
Everything else, however, goes to destruction along with the body. || 32 ||
For neither mother nor wife remains for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor friend, nor kinsman remains—only Dharma alone remains. (33)
Though powerful, such a person is powerless; though wealthy, he is destitute;
and though learned, he is a fool—anyone who is averse to Dharma.
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where no medicine exists, what will that sick man do? (35)
He who understands old age, death, fear, and disease is a wise man;
he may stand, sit, sleep, or laugh with anyone at all.
You see those of equal birth, age, and form being carried away by death;
yet you have no fear there, for your heart is like a diamond.

Thus it was said. Thereupon, having attained a state of detachment, King Vatsa said to Bhoja, "Forgive me," and after bowing down to him, he placed him upon a chariot. Leading him outside the city into the thick darkness, he brought him to his home, deposited him within an underground chamber, and thus protected Bhoja.

Having himself had the head of the Bhoja prince fashioned by experts in artificial arts—complete with beautiful earrings, a radiant face, and closed eyes—the youngest brother took it and went to the royal palace. Bowing to the king, he said, "That which was commanded by Your Majesty has been accomplished. Then the king, learning of his son's death, asked him, "Vatsarāja, what did that son say at the moment of the sword-stroke? Vatsa presented the letter. The king, having a lamp brought by his own wife's hand, read those letters on the leaf: "O King, this is the last word of your son; I am dying, struck by the sword of my enemy. May you be victorious! May my father be happy! May my mother be free from sorrow! And may the Queen Mother be ever devoted to her husband! The king, reading these words, fell to the ground in a swoon. When he regained consciousness, he cried out in grief, "Alas, my son! Alas, my son! and wept bitterly. Then the younger brother spoke to the king: "O King, do not grieve. This is the nature of worldly existence. All things are transitory. You have heard the teachings of the wise. Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, remain firm in your duty and govern the kingdom according to dharma. Thus consoled, the king performed the funeral rites for his son and ruled the earth. The younger brother, having achieved his purpose, returned to his own city. There he lived happily with his wife, enjoying all pleasures. Thus ends the story of the younger brother. It is said that one who hears this tale shall never suffer the loss of a son. May there be prosperity! Long live the King! Long live the Queen! Long live the Prince! Long live the Minister! Long live the City! Long live the Kingdom! Long live the People! Long live the World! Long live the Dharma! Long live the Truth! Long live the Virtue! Long live the Prosperity! Long live the Peace! Long live the Joy! Long live the Happiness! Long live the Liberation! Long live the Enlightenment! Long live the Omniscience! Long live the Universal Good! Long live the Supreme Bliss! Long live the Eternal Peace! Long live the Infinite Light! Long live the Unending Glory! Long live the Imperishable Fame! Long live the Undecaying Splendor! Long live the Unshakeable Sovereignty! Long live the Unconquerable Might! Long live the Unassailable Power! Long live the Unfailing Fortune! Long live the Unfading Beauty! Long live the Unblemished Purity! Long live the Unstained Integrity! Long live the Unwavering Devotion! Long live the Unbroken Faith! Long live the Unyielding Courage! Long live the Unfaltering Resolve! Long live the Unshakable Wisdom! Long live the Unerring Insight! Long live the Unconfused Discernment! Long live the Unclouded Knowledge! Long live the Unobstructed Vision! Long live the Unveiled Truth! Long live the Unhidden Reality! Long live the Unconcealed Essence! Long live the Unmasked Nature! Long live the Uncovered Mystery! Long live the Unsealed Secret! Long live the Unlocked Treasure! Long live the Unbarred Gate! Long live the Unfastened Door! Long live the Unbound Path! Long live the Unhindered Way! Long live the Unimpeded Progress! Long live the Unchecked Advancement! Long live the Unstalled Journey! Long live the Unhalted March! Long live the Unstopped Flight! Long live the Unrestrained Speed! Long live the Unrestrained Force! Long live the Unrestrained Energy! Long live the Unrestrained Power! Long live the Unrestrained Will! Long live the Unrestrained Action! Long live the Unrestrained Speech! Long live the Unrestrained Mind! Long live the Unrestrained Thought! Long live the Unrestrained Intention! Long live the Unrestrained Desire! Long live the Unrestrained Affection! Long live the Unrestrained Compassion! Long live the Unrestrained Love! Long live the Unrestrained Joy! Long live the Unrestrained Bliss! Long live the Unrestrained Peace! Long live the Unrestrained Tranquility! Long live the Unrestrained Serenity! Long live the Unrestrained Calm! Long live the Unrestrained Stability! Long live the Unrestrained Firmness! Long live the Unrestrained Constancy! Long live the Unrestrained Perseverance! Long live the Unrestrained Diligence! Long live the Unrestrained Endeavor! Long live the Unrestrained Effort! Long live the Unrestrained Striving! Long live the Unrestrained Exertion!
“King Māndhātṛ, who was the ornament of the Kṛta Age, has departed;
where is that destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa who constructed a bridge across the great ocean?
And other kings as well, beginning with Yudhiṣṭhira, have gone to heaven, O lord of the earth.”
O Muñja, this earth has never been shared by you with even a single person; she shall go [with you] alone.

When the king learned of this matter, he fell from his bed to the ground. Then, regaining consciousness through the breeze from the hem of the queen’s lotus-hand garment, he cried out, “Queen! Do not touch me! Alas, alas! I am a slayer of my own son! Lamenting thus like a kurara bird, he summoned the doorkeepers and said, “Bring the brahmins here!”

Then, having bowed to the Brahmins who had assembled by his command, he said, "I have killed my son; prescribe for me the expiation for that. To him, who was speaking thus, they replied, "O King, enter the fire immediately. Thereupon, Buddhisāgara approached and said, "Just as you are the lowest of kings, so too is Vatsarāja the lowest of ministers. Having indeed given you the kingdom, that King Sindhula established the Bhoja on your lap; yet your paternal uncle has treated it otherwise."
In youth, which lasts but a few days and brings intoxication, the wicked commit such offenses that their very birth becomes in vain. (39)
The virtuous consider the removal of a blade of grass from their heads to be equal to the gift of ten million gold pieces;
whereas the wicked, even when their assistance has been rendered at the cost of their own lives, carry it as if it were enmity.
For one whose heart is like stone, for whom both benefit and harm are forgotten, the designation "living" is in vain. (41)
Just as a sprout, though extremely minute, when protected with care will yield fruit in due time, so too does the world when well-protected. 42.
Gold, grain, jewels, and various kinds of wealth, as well as whatever else belongs to the subjects, should belong to the rulers of the earth. (43)
When the queen is righteous, those around her are always most righteous; when she is sinful, they are ever devoted to sin.
The subjects always follow the king; as is the king, so are the subjects.

Then, when the king had decided to enter the fire that very night, all the vassal lords and citizens gathered together, and a rumor spread everywhere: "The king, terrified by the fear of sin for having killed his son, is entering the fire. Thereupon, Buddhisāgara summoned the doorkeeper and, after declaring, "No one is to enter the royal palace," he settled the king in the inner apartments and sat alone in the assembly hall.

Then, having heard the news of the king’s death, the King of Vatsa entered the assembly hall, bowed to Buddhisāgara, and said softly, “Father, I have protected the King of Bhoja. Buddhisāgara whispered something into his ear; having heard this, the King of Vatsa departed.

Then, after a moment, a certain Kāpālika arrived at the assembly, holding the tusk of a lordly elephant in his hand, having fashioned a fresh mass of matted hair, his entire body smeared with ash mixed with camphor like the god of love incarnate, his pair of ears adorned with crystal earrings, wearing a silken loincloth, and appearing like the moon-crested Śiva in bodily form. Seeing him, Buddhisāgara said: "O Lord of Yogins, from where have you come? And where is your dwelling?"
“In you, a Kāpālika, there exists a particular art that causes wonder, as well as a particular medicinal herb. The Yogin replied:
“In every land there is a dwelling, and likewise in every house there is alms-food;
in every lake and river there is water—Śiva, Śiva!—for those men who are yogins of the true reality. (45)
In every village there is a charming hut, at every waterfall there is water, and food is easily obtained through alms; what need is there for worldly riches? (46)

"Your Majesty, we do not belong to a single region; we wander over the entire circle of the earth. We abide by the instructions of our Guru. We behold the whole surface of the world as clearly as an amalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand. O Father, whether one is bitten by a snake, overwhelmed by poison, seized by disease, pierced in the head by a weapon, or rendered frail by old age—at that very moment, we rid them of the entire accumulation of their ailments."

The king, having heard the entire account while remaining hidden behind a wall, entered the assembly hall and prostrated himself like a staff before the Kāpālika, saying: “O Lord of Yogins, you who are like Rudra and devoted to the service of others, protect me by granting life to my son, who was killed by me, a great sinner. Then the Kāpālika replied: “O King, do not fear; your son shall not die. By the grace of Śiva, he will return home.”

"Furthermore, send the materials for the fire sacrifice to the cremation ground along with Buddhisāgara," he said. Then the king sent Buddhisāgara with the command, "Do everything exactly as the Kāpālika has instructed. Thereafter, during the night, Bhoja was also led there to the riverbank in secret guise. And a rumor spread that "Bhoja has been restored to life by the yogin."

Then King Bhoja, mounted upon a lordly elephant, being praised by bards and deafening the world with the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and other instruments, went to the royal palace surrounded by his citizens and ministers. The king embraced him and wept. Bhoja, in turn, consoled the weeping Muñja and offered him praise. Thereupon, the gratified king seated him upon his own throne, adorned him with the royal parasol and fly-whisks, and bestowed the kingdom upon him.

Having granted one village to each of his sons, he established Jayanta—the object of his supreme affection—in the position of crown prince (*bhojanikāśe*). Then, having secured his salvation for the next world, Muñja also went to the forest of asceticism with his principal queens and performed supreme penance. Thereafter, King Bhoja governed the kingdom through the grace of the gods and the Brahmins.
Thus concludes the narrative of King Bhoja’s accession to the throne.

Then, having appointed his chief minister Buddhisāgara as regent, King Bhojarāja enjoyed his own kingdom once Muñja had departed for the penance grove. As time passed in this manner, one day while the king was going to a garden to sport, he noticed a certain Brahmin resident of Dhārānagara. Seeing the king, that man approached with his eyes closed; being questioned by the king, he said: "O twice-born one, why do you not utter 'svasti' upon seeing me? Moreover, you close your eyes specifically; what is the reason for this?"

The Brahmin said: “O King, you are a devotee of Viṣṇu; you will not cause harm to the Brahmins, and therefore I have no fear of you. However, you give nothing to anyone; thus, you possess not even the name of ‘generosity. So what is the use of your benediction? Furthermore, my eyes are closed according to the worldly proverb that ‘by looking at the face of a beggar in the morning, one suffers a loss of gain thereafter. Moreover— ‘He whose favor is fruitless and whose anger is likewise useless—’”
Subjects do not desire such a king, just as women do not desire a eunuch.
The learning of one who lacks confidence, the wealth of a miser, and the strength of the arm of a coward—these three are useless on this earth. (48)

"Your Majesty, my aged father, while traveling toward Kāśī, was asked by me for advice: 'Father, what should I do? My father replied to me thus: 'O wise one, even in your dreams, you must never serve a king whose heart is conquered by his ministers, conquered by eunuchs, or conquered by young women. (49)
"O dear one, among all sins there are two supreme sins:
first, a king who has a wicked minister, and second, one who takes refuge with him. (50)

Where the king possesses a mind devoid of discernment, where the minister turns his neck away from the virtuous, and where the wicked are powerful—how can there be any occasion for the presence of the good? (51)

Even if a king is devoid of prosperity, he should be served if he is a repository of qualities worthy of service; for from him comes a livelihood, and even after a long interval of time, a fruit [of that service] arises.

There is no nobility in one who does not give. Your Majesty, just as in the past kings such as Karṇa, Dadhīci, Śibi, and Vikrama, by adorning the next world with the divine new qualities born of their own generosity, continue to dwell upon the circle of the earth—do others do the same?
When the body is perishable, what protection is there? One’s fame is that which must be protected, for it is imperishable.
A man, though his physical body has fallen, lives on through the body of his fame. (53)
Death is equal toward everyone: toward the wise and the fool, the strong and the weak, the lord and the poor. (54)
Even for a mere moment, your life does not remain as it passes away;
therefore, one should acquire fame alone amidst these impermanent bodies. (55)
Even that life which is devoid of knowledge, valor, arts, noble shame, renunciation, and enjoyment is considered fruitless by the virtuous; how much more so for men [who possess these]? (56)

The king, as if bathed in a flood of nectar and as if merged into the Supreme Brahman by those words, shed tears of joy from his eyes. And he said to the twice-born man: "O best of brahmins, listen—In this world, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are rare indeed. (57)
Those who are wise are not necessarily well-wishers, and those who are well-wishers are not necessarily wise.
Even a learned friend is rare for men, just as medicine that is both palatable and beneficial is rare. (58)

Having given a hundred thousand [gold pieces] to the brahmin, the king asked, "What is your name? The brahmin wrote his own name on the ground: "Govinda. The king, having read it, said, "Brahmin, you must come to the royal palace every day. There shall be no restriction upon you. Learned men and poets are to be brought to the assembly out of curiosity. Indeed, let no learned man suffer any hardship; maintain this office," he said.
Thus, as some days passed, the king—who was fond of the learned and a lord of wealth—honored him as such.

Fame spread abroad. Then, desiring to see the king, sages arrived from various directions. While the king was thus expending his wealth and resources, the chief minister once addressed him as follows: "O Lord, kings are victorious only through the strength of their treasury, and not otherwise.
'The earth belongs to him who possesses excellent elephants;
he who has a treasury is invincible, and he who has a fortress is unconquerable. (59)

"O King, behold the world—generally, the thirst for wealth is strongest among those who already possess it. Observe how a bow fixed at two crores [of gold] bends toward a mere hundred thousand. || 60 ||
Thus the king said to him:
"Wealth that is barren of both giving and enjoyment, which is not shared by friends, though acquired by a man, gradually becomes misfortune. (61)

Having spoken thus, the king dismissed that minister from his office and appointed another in his place. And he said to him: "A hundred thousand [gold pieces] should be given to a great poet, half of that to a learned scholar;
one village should be given for half of that, and half of that again to one who requests it. (62)
And whoever intends to prohibit my distribution [of wealth] among ministers and others must be killed. For it is said:
"That which one gives away and that which one eats—that alone is the wealth of the wealthy;
others play with even the wife and the riches of the deceased. (63)
He was beloved by his subjects as a giver, and not merely as the lord of wealth;
for it is the rain-cloud that people desire when it gives, and not the ocean, even though it holds water.
Even the ocean, though usually intent solely on gathering [water] within the depths of the netherworld, becomes a giver when it sees the cloud thundering above the world. 65.

Having heard that King Bhoja was thus distinguished for his generosity, a certain poet from the land of Kaliṅga arrived and remained for a month; yet he did not obtain an audience with the lord of the earth, nor did he even have provisions for his journey to sustain himself. Then one day, the king went out, desiring to hunt. Seeing the king, the poet said:
"When the illustrious King Bhoja is seen, three things instantly dissolve:
the weapon of the enemy, the distress of the poet, and the girdle-fastening of deer-eyed women. (66)

The king gave him one hundred thousand. Then, while that king was fond of hunting, a certain son of the Pulindas sang; pleased by the sweetness of his song, the king gave five hundred thousand to that son of the Pulindas. At that time, the poet, seeing that gift so exalted and the young Kirāta, addressed the king under the guise of the lotus resting in the king’s lotus-hand:
"O lotus, these virtues of yours, though they exist, do not come to light; for the treasury of you, who are the abode of Lakṣmī, is enjoyed by bees. (67)
King Bhoja, having understood that intention, gave him another hundred thousand. Then the king said to the brahmin:
"O Brahmin, it is skill alone that is honored by masters, not noble birth;
one possessed of skill is placed upon the head by Śambhu, even above the gods. (68)

While the King of Bhoja was speaking thus, five or six poets arrived from somewhere. Upon seeing them, the king appeared embarrassed, thinking, "I have already given away so much wealth today. Then, the poet, perceiving the king's intention, spoke again to him under the guise of addressing a lotus:
"Why are you angry with someone? Be angry instead with your own honey, for whose sake the bees are now searching through every petal of you, O hundred-petaled one? (69)
Then, observing the Lord’s serene countenance, Prakāśa said:
"A miser is unable either to give away or to enjoy his wealth;
he merely touches it with his hand, like a eunuch touching a woman. (70)
"He who rejoices when asked [for a gift], and who feels joy after having given—it is by seeing or even hearing of such a man that another person attains heaven. (71)

Then the king, being pleased, gave another hundred thousand to the three inhabitants of the Kaliṅga country. Thereupon, the first poet, seeing the six eminent poets standing before him, said: "O poets, when the king—who resides here on the site of the great lake and the bridge—goes to his palace, then say something. And all those great poets, having understood the king's initial intention, turned back. Among them, one spoke to the king under the pretext of the lake:
"To those who have arrived but are not yet full, and to those who are full but are departing..."
That lake is superior where there is no clashing of jars upon its path. || 72 ||
Thus he spoke; the king gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Then, seeing those lords of poets, Govinda Paṇḍita became enraged.
Perceiving his intention to be angry, the second poet said:
"Whose thirst do you not quench? Who does not drink your water after entering within?"
If he were not a crocodile in the lake of the True Path, he would not dwell within its embrace. || 73 ||

The king gave him two hundred thousand [gold pieces] and, having removed Govinda Paṇḍita from his office of administration, said: "You too must come to the assembly, but no one should act with malice. Having spoken thus and given one hundred thousand to each of them, he returned to his own city. They, for their part, departed as they had come. Then, on a certain occasion, the king said to his chief minister:
"Even a Brahmin who is a fool should be outside my city."
“Let even that wise potter remain in my city. || 74 ||
Thus, there was no fool whatsoever in the city of Dhārā;

consequently, in due course, five hundred scholars—including Vararuci, Bāṇa, Mayūra, Rephaṇa, Hari, Śaṅkara, Kaliṅga, Karpūra, Vināyaka, Madana, Vidyāvinoda, Kokila, Tārendra, and others—all of whom were experts in every branch of learning and possessed of omniscience, graced the court of King Śrī Bhoja.

While matters stood thus, once, as the Lord of Bhoja—the crest-jewel of poets, lover of poetry, and dear friend of brahmins—was seated upon his lion-throne which was worshipped by throngs of scholars, the doorkeeper approached, prostrated, and informed him: “Your Majesty, a certain scholar stands at the gate. Then, when the King commanded, “Let him enter,” that brahmin, shining with his right hand raised high, said: “O King, may there be prosperity!
The King asked, “Śaṅkaraka, what is this in the letter?
The poet replied, “A verse.”
The king said,
"O poet, [recite] yours. The King [replied], "O Lord of the Earth, let that be recited."
The Poet says: "It is recited:

'Let the jingling of the bracelets on the creeper-like arms of these women with eyes as beautiful as lotuses, which momentarily quiver from the sudden waving of chowries, be stopped for a moment. (75)
The more Bhoja’s fame increases, as if striving to turn the three worlds white,
the more my heart is tormented by the fear that my beloved’s dark tresses might become pale.

Then the king gave one million two hundred thousand [gold pieces] to Śaṅkaraka. All the learned men became dejected in countenance; however, out of fear of the king, no one spoke. When the king had gone home on account of some business, the assembly of wise men, seeing the court devoid of ornaments, censured him: "Oh, the ignorance of this monarch! What is the use of serving him? He gave a hundred thousand to poets who were his own dependents, though they were experts in the Vedas and Shastras. What is the point of being pleased with such a man?"

"And that Śaṅkara is merely a vulgar poet; what is his audacity?"—when such clamor had arisen, a certain man approached, adorned with earrings of gold and jewels, draped in divine garments like a prince, his body smeared with musk-paste, his head honored with fresh flowers, alluring with sandalwood unguent like the personified God of Love (Vilāsa), having assumed a physical form like Poetry itself, vibrating like a flow of the erotic sentiment (Śṛṅgāra-rasa), and like Mahendra [descending] upon the circle of the earth.

The learned man arrived. Upon seeing him, that assembly of scholars became a vessel for both fear and curiosity. He prostrated before them all and asked, "Where is King Bhoja? They replied to him, "He has just now gone inside the palace. Then, having offered betel to each of them, he sat like a lion among a herd of lordly elephants.

Then that great man, perceiving that they had been deceived by the gift of the Śaṅkara-kavi, said: "You must not think that twelve hundred thousand were given to the Śaṅkara-kavi; rather, the king’s true intention was not understood by you. For when the worship of Śaṅkara was commenced, the Śaṅkara-kavi was honored with only a single hundred thousand."

"But having perceived those other forms—the eleven Rudras and Śaṅkaras—who are devoted to him and resplendent with his name as being directly present, the poet Śaṅkara himself offered one hundred thousand [verses] for each of them to that form of Śaṅkara; such was the king’s intention. Everyone was filled with wonder by this.

Then a certain royal officer immediately reported that scholar’s true nature to the king. And the king, regarding that great man—who had directly perceived his own intention—as being like Maheśvara himself, entered the assembly hall. He, for his part, said "Svasti" to the king.

The king embraced him and, having bowed and taken his lotus-like hand with his own lotus-like hand, went into the interior of the palace. Seated at a lofty window, he said: "O Brahmin, by which syllables of your name is good fortune supported? Or in which land does separation from you afflict the virtuous? Then the poet wrote "Kālidāsa" on the king's hand. Having read it, the king fell at his feet.
Then, while Kālidāsa and King Bhoja were seated there, evening arrived. The king said to his friend, "Describe the twilight. Kālidāsa replied:
"Like learning in one addicted to vice, the beauty of the lotuses fades; like bees in a foreign land, they fall into a state of wretchedness;
and like a wicked king, the darkness afflicts the world."
Like the wealth of a miser, his sight comes to naught. || 77 ||
Furthermore, the poet praises the king:
"Courtesy should be observed as long as men have not yet developed friendship;
for those in whom friendship has arisen, courtesy becomes hypocrisy. (78)
By him the entire earth, filled with gold, was given to the poets—he who understands the divine composition of excellent poetry and the sequence of the poets. (79)
No one other than a true poet understands the poetic excellence of a good poet’s words; for a barren woman does not recognize the supreme state of longing pregnancy.
Thus it was said. Thereupon, in due course, affection arose between Bhoja and Kālidāsa.

Then, perceiving that Kālidāsa was addicted to courtesans, everyone harbored hatred toward him; no one would even touch him. Once, having observed Kālidāsa in the midst of the assembly, Bhoja thought to himself, "How is it that even this wise man suffers the distraction of love's torment? He too, understanding his intention, replied: "In the context of the restless play of the mind-born god [Cupid], what talk can there be of those who dwell in the world of mortals?"
Such was the prowess of that conqueror of cities, who was formerly of a fiery nature, that it lasted for only half a month.
Then King Bhoja, being pleased, gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every syllable.
Thereupon, Kālidāsa praised Bhoja:
"O Great King, illustrious one, since the world has been whitened by your fame..."
This Supreme Person seeks the ocean from its near shore to its far shore;
Śiva seeks Kailāsa; the wielder of the thunderbolt seeks his celestial elephant; Rāhu seeks the moon; and Brahmā now seeks the swan.
Having drawn water and milk from all the oceans, the lotus-born Brahmā traverses them; yet Mukunda, the wielder of the discus, wanders over all the seas while holding his discus.
Paśupati, beholding them with his eye in his forehead, consumes all the lofty mountains.
O King Bhojarāja, lord of the earth, the lovely lady that is your fame pervades the three worlds.
O crest-jewel of learned kings, having observed your fame and Mount Kailāsa, the Creator, desiring to balance them, placed the mountain on one side; to complete the weight,
he placed upon it the bull that accompanies Umā, and upon the bull’s head, the waters of the Gaṅgā.
In front of that [seat], he should visualize a preeminent serpent, and above that, the expansive moon.
"O cowherd, where are you going from heaven? O divine sage, do you wish to bring the calf of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) to the earth now to gather grass? O simpleton, she has no milk.

Having heard this, the cow—her udders dried up with shame at King Bhoja’s abundant generosity—thought, "My labor would indeed be in vain; for even that [grass] has been chewed up entirely by his enemies. (85)
The king, being pleased, gave a hundred thousand coins for every single syllable.

Then, on one occasion, certain scholars who had mastered the Vedas and the Smṛtis, knowing the king to be fond of poetry, sat down outside a city, thinking, "By the grace of Bhuvaneśvarī, we shall compose poetry. Among them, one who considered himself a scholar recited a quarter-verse:
"O Indra among kings, give us food!"
Thus it was recited. Another read: "Accompanied by ghee and broth.

The second half of the verse did not occur to him. Thereupon, Kālidāsa went to the temple of the deity to pay his respects. Seeing him, the twice-born said: "Although we are knowers of the entire Veda, Bhoja grants us nothing at all; yet he bestows whatever is desired upon those such as yourself. Therefore, we have come here with the intention of composing poetry. We have deliberated for a long time and uttered the first half; now, having composed the second half, please give it to us."
Saying, "Then he will give us something," she spoke half a verse in his presence. And he, having heard that, [recited]:
"And buffalo curd, white as the moonlight of the autumnal moon. (86)

Thus he spoke. They went to the royal palace and said to the doorkeepers, "We have come having composed a poem; show us to the king. Out of curiosity, they laughed and, having gone and bowed to the king, said:
"O King of Kings, at the gate stand those who know the Vedic meters—enemies of the *śloka*—with teeth like black gram and hands placed upon their hips. (87)

Thus it was said. Having been ushered in by the king, they entered the royal assembly and, having gathered together, recited their poetry all at once. Upon hearing this, the king realized that the second half had been composed by Kālidāsa; he then addressed the Brahmins: "Never again shall poetry be produced from the mouth of him who caused the first half to be made. A certain reward shall be given for the second half, but nothing for the first. Having said this, he gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every single syllable.
When they had departed after receiving their rewards, the king looked at Kālidāsa and said, "O poet, you have composed the second half. The poet replied:
"The sweetness of the lower lip, the firmness of the breasts, and the sharpness of the eyes—only one who relishes experience truly understands the perfection of poetry. (88)
And the king said, "O good poet, you speak the truth!
An unprecedented flavor shines forth in the fruit of the nectar of poetry from the Goddess of Speech."
In the tasting of the universal commonality, the true poet alone possesses the discernment for its sweetness. || 89 ||
Having reflected again and again upon the entire world, three things have entered my heart:
the transformations of sugarcane, the thoughts of poets, and the undulating side-glances of beautiful women. (90)

Then, on one occasion, the gatekeeper, having prostrated before the Bhoja king, said: "O King, a certain poet named Lakṣmīdhara from the Draviḍa country stands at the gate. The king said, "Let him enter. Seeing him enter, shining like the sun, and having long remained without his purpose being known, the king reflected and said: "Blessed are those who, having had their desires fulfilled merely by discerning the outward appearance [of a petitioner], never hear the piteous words of supplicants anywhere. (91)

Having arrived there, he greeted the king with "May it be well" and, sitting down by the king's command, said: "O Lord, this assembly of yours is adorned by the wise, and you yourself are Viṣṇu in person. Therefore, what need is there for scholarship? Nevertheless, I shall say something:

Having created the majesty of Bhoja, did the Creator fashion the thunderbolt in the hand of Indra, the sun in the sky, and the submarine fire in the belly of the ocean from the remaining atoms that were cast aside? (92)

Thus it was said. Thereupon, he was honored by the assembly, and the king granted him a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every single syllable. Again the poet said: "O King, I have come here with my family in the hope of finding a place to dwell.
A master who is patient, generous, and appreciative of merit is found through one's own virtue;
yet a poet who is well-disposed, pure, skillful, and learned is exceedingly rare. (93)

Thus it was said. Then the king spoke to his chief minister: “Let a house be given to him. Thereupon, having searched the entire city, the minister could not find any fool whom he might displace so that the house could be given to the learned man. Wandering everywhere, he saw the house of a certain weaver and said to the weaver: “Weaver, leave your house; a scholar shall come for it.”

Then the weaver, having reached the royal palace and bowed before the king, said: "O King, your minister treats me as a fool and is casting me out from my home; you must judge whether I am a fool or a scholar.
I compose poetry, yet I do not produce it very well; I work with great effort, and if I do so, I produce it even more beautifully."
O King, whose footstool is adorned by the crest-jewels of sovereigns, O Sāhasāṅka, I speak, I weave, and I go forth [in song]. 94.

Then the king said to the weaver, who was speaking with words of praise: “Your line of verse is charming and the sweetness of your poetry is beautiful; however, poetry should be spoken after due deliberation. Thereupon, the weaver, becoming angry, said: “O King, an answer occurs to me here, but I do not speak it; for the duty of a king is distinct from the duty of a learned man. The king said: “If there is an answer, then speak it.”
The weaver said: "O King, I consider no other poet to be equal to Kālidāsa. Who else in your assembly is a scholar who knows the true essence of poetry, apart from Kālidāsa?
That splendor of Sarasvatī which arises from the ripening of the nectar of the Guru’s grace can be attained only by a poet; it is certainly not for those who rely on the prestige of rote recitation."
Even though it dwells all day long in a lake and makes the expanse of water utterly muddy, does the buffalo ever acquire the fragrance of the lotus pond? (95)
This composition of mine, sweet with the cleverness of its lucid words and radiant in its structure,
is fruitless in the heart of another but finds its fulfillment in the heart of a poet—
just as the sidelong glance of a fair-eyed woman, falling from eyes half-closed at the corners, is wasted on one but meaningful for the beloved.
"In the prince it is essence-less, yet it somehow delights the youth.
Thus spoke Sītā, who is revered by the wise:
"The fool does not grieve over his own stupidity when a poem worthy of those with expansive hearts suffers."
A woman with withered breasts generally blames only her bodice. || 97 ||

Then the weaver said: "In childhood for one's sons, in lovemaking for women, in praise for poets, and in battle for warriors—speech joined with the word 'thou' (tvaṃ) is indeed lauded. What is this burden of delusion upon you, O Lord? Remember yourself! (98)
Then the king, saying, "Excellent, O weaver!", gave him a hundred thousand coins (*akṣaralakṣa*). He spoke again to the weaver: "Do not be afraid."

In this manner, after some time had passed, Bāṇa, the best of scholars, although highly honored by the king, continued to experience poverty due to his past karma. While things stood thus, the king once wandered through his own city at night alone in disguise and arrived at Bāṇa’s house. Then, at midnight, Bāṇa, distressed by his poverty, said to his wife: “My lady, how many times has the king fulfilled my heart’s desire? Even now, when requested again, he surely grants it.”
"But even the tongue of a fool becomes numbed by the flavor of constant prayer. Having said this, he remained silent for half a moment. Then he recited again:
"Hara! Hara! O Destroyer of the Cities! What is the harshness of the words of a beggar compared to the poison Halāhala?
Your single tongue of taste alone knows the relative intensity of the flavor of fearlessness [found therein]. (99)
O Goddess, begging is another form of poverty; it is not merely a lack of wealth.
Even though Śambhu was clad only in a loincloth, he remained the Supreme Lord.

Service is the ruin of pleasures, begging is the ruin of wealth, a wicked king is the ruin of subjects, and a son of corrupt character is the ruin of families—a harsh axe that strikes at the very root. 101.
Therefore, even though he is poor, it is impossible for me to speak of the king myself;
for while the cloud becomes beloved by all the world in an instant,
the sun, though constantly extending its rays, causes only torment.

Moreover, O Queen, it is this that burns my heart: that those who arrive at the time of the Vaiśvadeva offering, afflicted by hunger, depart afterwards. The heat of the fire of poverty has been quenched by the water of contentment;
but by what can the internal burning caused by the frustration of the hopes of supplicants be extinguished? (103)
When the king had heard all this, he said, "It is not appropriate to give anything now; I shall fulfill Bāṇa’s desire at dawn itself," and then the king departed, saying:

"Of what use are those poetic compositions, those armies, or those riches, by which no one was made eloquent, by which no one was freed from calamity, by which no one was granted a position, and by which no petitioner was treated as one's own equal? (104)

While the king was thus wandering through the city, two thieves were traveling along the road. One of them, Śakunta, said: "Friend, although the world is spread over with vast darkness, by the power of my collyrium I see everywhere everything, even down to the finest atoms. However, even this mass of gold brought from the storehouse does not bring me any pleasure."

The second thief, named Marāla, said: "For what reason is it said that even the collection of gold brought from the storehouse is not beneficial? Thereupon Śakunta replied: "City guards are patrolling everywhere; everyone will be awakened by the sound of their kettledrums, tabors, and other instruments. Therefore, having divided what was brought and taken the wealth belonging to each person's own share, we must depart immediately. Marāla said: "Friend, what will you do with this collection of jewels and gold amounting to twenty million?"

The bird said: “I shall give this wealth to some twice-born man so that he, having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, will not seek another. The swan replied: “Friend Cāru, if a thrill of joy arises while one is giving, fighting, or studying...”
That gift, which pertains to both oneself and others, is known as the heroic (pauruṣa) gift. || 105 ||
"How will there be any fruit of merit for you from this gift?
The bird said: "This is our ancestral tradition, that wealth is brought here by means of theft.
The swan said: "How can even all the wealth acquired at the risk of one's own life be given away?"
Śakunta said: "A fool does not give wealth out of fear of poverty;
but a wise man gives away wealth out of fear of poverty. (106)
Marāla said: "One vessel consists of the Vedas, and another vessel consists of austerity;
but the most excellent of all vessels is he in whose stomach there is no food belonging to a Śūdra. (107)

Śakunta: "What will you do with this wealth? Marāla: "Friend, a certain young Brahmin residing in Kāśī has come here. He described the fruits of dwelling in Kāśī before our father. Consequently, our father—who has been committing theft since childhood—having desisted from his sin by the power of fate and through world-weariness, will go to Kāśī together with his family. This collection of money is for that purpose.
Śakunta: "Great indeed is the fortune of your father! For instance:"
Does the wretched Indra, whose soul is perfumed by the latent impression of dwelling in the city of Vārāṇasī, attain equality with a dog? 108.
The city of Vārāṇasī is a field for the crops of karma that is otherwise barren;
there, liberation is attained equally by both the outcaste and the scholar. (109)
Where death is auspicious, where opulence is the ornament, and where a loincloth is silk—by whom can that Kāśī be measured? (110)
Having heard this dialogue between the two, the king was delighted and reflected in his mind: "The course of mental actions is altogether wondrous; the intellect of both is indeed pure.

Then the king, having turned back, saw his father and son within the palace. There, the father said to his son: "Now, although the king has understood the true essence of the scriptures, he gives nothing out of stinginess.
Rather—he composes poetry when the petitioner composes poetry, and recites when the petitioner recites; he offers praise when the petitioner is intent on praise."
Afterwards, when "I shall go" is said, the silent one closes his eyes. || 111 ||

The king, having heard this, approached him and said, "Do not speak thus," and having removed all the ornaments from his own body, he gave them to him. Then, returning home and sitting in the assembly hall at a later time, he said to Kālidāsa: "Friend, 'I bow to the minds of poets, which cross over upon the waters of their creative intuition (pratibhā).
Thereupon the poet replied:"
"Wherein the fourteen worlds are like swans and birds. || 112 ||
Then the king gave a hundred thousand pearls for every single syllable.

Thereupon, the doorkeeper enters: “Your Majesty, a certain scholar, possessing nothing but a loincloth, stands at the gate. The king says, “Let him enter. Once he has been ushered in, the poet approaches, says “May there be well-being,” and sits down without being told; he then speaks: “Mount Meru, the crest-jewel of all mountains, dwells here; indeed, the seven oceans have deposited their burdens here.”
This incomparable and infinite surface of the earth, capable of supporting the emergence of many living beings, is the proper place for those such as us.
"O King Mahākavi, what is your name? Please tell me. The Poet: "It is not proper for scholars to mention their names. Nevertheless, I shall speak if you know [how to listen].
For an intellect still nursing at the breast does not fathom profound speech."
There is indeed no bamboo staff with which one can see the bottom of the ocean.
O King, listen—

the daughter of the mountain, her face radiant with laughter, has taken the crescent moon fallen from the sky and the bracelet broken in a lovers' quarrel, and joined them together into a single circle.
He said, "Look!"— may that Giriśa protect you, along with Girijā and that moon of his sport, whose body is overspread by the rays of his teeth.
Kālidāsa: "Friend Krīḍācandra, it is a long time since we have seen you. How is it that you are in such a state, even though the king—though possessed of great wealth—is reigning over the realm?
Krīḍācandra:
"Even those who possess wealth are counted among the foremost of the truly destitute if they lack the power to give."
Since it does not quench thirst, even the ocean is nothing but a desert.
Moreover:
For those men who are averse to enjoyment and intent solely on the accumulation of wealth, their riches remain in the house for the sake of another, like a jewel of a maiden. (117)
O Bhoja, a connoisseur of essence attains their very status through mere skill alone, whereas other kings possess it only through the ostentation of golden ornaments and jeweled armlets.
Poems that are naturally charming even without the addition of clever artifice distill nectar as if they were made of nectar itself, just like the youth of courtesans.
The name of a king is never known at all without his poetry;
likewise, without that [poetry], the fame of a poet does not shine upon the earth. (120)
Mayūra:
"Those are to be revered, those are great-souled ones, and their fame remains firm in the world—those by whom poems have been composed, and those who have been celebrated in poetry. (121)
Vararuci:
On this path of poets, which is charming due to the bonds of connoisseurs manifested through the clarity of words and meanings, the intellect of the wise alone shines forth.
Moreover, this path of the sidelong glances of noble women does not betray even a trace of addiction to sport; it is indeed beyond the domain of courtesans.
The king gave Krīḍācandra twenty lordly elephants and five hundred villages; then the poet praised the king:
"A bracelet upon the pair of eyes, a tilaka-mark upon the sprout-like hand..."
Oh, how wonderful is the variety of ornaments upon the wives of Bhoja's enemies!
The king, being pleased, gave him another hundred thousand coins.
Then, on one occasion, a certain scholar named Rāmeśvara, whose every limb and joint was worn out by old age, entered the assembly hall. He said:
"By the royal glory of the great poet Pañcānana, through the elephant meat..."
For one who observes a fast everywhere, the breaking of the fast occurs only on rare occasions.
Just as there is another person who takes charge of horses and scholars, so too the king is the supreme taker of lordly poets and lordly elephants. 125.
For thus:
"The beauty of courtesans consists of gold and silken garments;
the sons of kings shine through valor and generosity. (126)
Having heard this, the king removed all his ornaments and bestowed two hundred thousand [gold pieces] upon the scholar Rāmeśvara.
Then the poet praises him:
"O Bhoja, for the sake of your wife, Fame, there is a great [mirror] situated upon the forehead of the sky."
O King, O mine of virtues, your musk-tilaka shines resplendently. || 127 ||
One should not speak of virtues in the presence of the wise, because they already know them well for themselves;
nor should one speak of them in the presence of fools, for they do not understand what has been proclaimed by the wise. 128.
Everyone was struck with wonder by that.
Rāmeśvara Kavi said: "A virtuous man brings about fame; a true poet merely composes poetry."
The sun nourishes the lotus and endows it with beauty.
Thereupon, the king, being pleased, gave a lac of coins for every single syllable. The poet, O lord of kings, said:
"A miser, devoid of fame, does not hear poetry at all; what can a eunuch do even when a gazelle-eyed woman stands before him? (130)
Sītā said:
“Those wretched poets and even those elephants have been destroyed by Your Majesty; no splendor arises for them without the palace of a sovereign of the realm. (131)
Kālidāsa:
"The words of a poet never touch the heart of one who is ungenerous;
the amorous charms of a young woman serve only for the sorrow of an elderly man. (132)
The king granted a reward of one hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every learned scholar.

Then, on one occasion, observing that Kālidāsa was superior even to the entire circle of poets, the king felt a slight pang of regret in his heart due to his extreme infatuation with courtesans. At that time, Sītā—who is revered by the assembly of the wise—perceiving his intention, said: "O King, those who delight in virtue do not feel dejected even upon seeing a fault in a person possessed of merit."
Out of affection alone, the world perceives even the spot on the moon as a beauty.

The king, being pleased, gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces] to Sītā; yet, when he still did not honor Kālidāsa as before, Kālidāsa, having discerned the king’s intention, spoke under the pretext of a balance: "O Balance, having attained the status of a standard of measurement, who indeed remains indifferent to you?
You cast that which is weightiest down below, while you raise the other much higher. (134)
He spoke again:
"Why does he who has access everywhere suffer distress out of attachment to his own country?
Calling this well 'my father's,' base men drink its salty water. (135)
Then, perceiving in his mind the contempt shown by the king, Kālidāsa went to his own home with a heavy heart.
For who is able to reconcile love shattered by contempt?
A pearl that has cracked cannot be joined again by an application of lac. (136)

Then the king also remained there, dejected. Seeing the king distressed, Līlāvatī asked him the cause of his despondency. The king told her everything in private. Having learned from the king's own mouth of the contempt shown toward Kālidāsa, she spoke again: "O Lord, my life-breath, you are all-knowing. For unfulfilled affection is better than affection that has been broken. One who has had his eyes stolen away may indeed be sorrowful, but one born blind does not become sorrowful. (137)
But Kālidāsa is a certain incarnation of the Goddess of Speech in human form; therefore, honor him with your whole being before the learned. Behold:
though he is a maker of darkness, though he is crooked, though he is marked by a stain, and though his rising is ordained at the time of the sun's setting—
Nevertheless, the moon still attains the status of being beloved by Hara;
indeed, there can be no deliberation regarding merits or faults among those who have sought refuge.
The king, accepting this by saying, "My dear, all of this is indeed true," declared, "Tomorrow morning, I shall satisfy Kālidāsa."

On another day, the king, having performed his morning rites such as brushing his teeth and completed his daily obligations, arrived at the assembly hall. The scholars, poets, singers, and all the other courtiers gathered there. Observing that Kālidāsa alone had not yet arrived, the king dispatched one of his servants to the courtesan’s house to summon him. That servant went, bowed to Kālidāsa, and said: "O Lord of Poets, the King of Bhoja summons you.
Then the poet reflected: "Yesterday I was insulted by the king; what could be the reason for summoning me so early this morning?"
Whomever the king honors with affection in the assembly, for the sake of displacing each such person, the king’s favorites strive. (169)

But especially, while I am being honored daily by the king, these deceitful men incite enmity out of malice. Where the king’s mind lacks discernment, where the minister is hostile toward the virtuous, and where the wicked are powerful—how can there be any opportunity for the good? (140)

Reflecting thus, he entered the assembly hall. Then, seeing him approaching from afar, he rose joyfully from his seat and, saying, "O good poet, my dearest friend, why do you delay today? he walked five or six steps toward him. Thereupon, the entire assembly rose from their seats, and all the members were filled with wonder; meanwhile, the faces of his adversaries became pale.

Then the king, taking Bāṇa’s lotus-like hand with his own lotus-like hand, led him to his own seat, seated him upon the throne, and at his command sat down there himself. When Kālidāsa had thus ascended the royal throne, the poet Bāṇa raised his right arm and said: “Through his honoring of Kālidāsa, Bhoja has become a king among the wise—a Rudra of the arts—even though he is [otherwise] like the moon, the maker of darkness. (141)

Thereupon, the fire of enmity toward him blazed up even more intensely among the learned. Then, after some wise men had consulted together, all the scholars honored Bhoja’s betel-bearer, a maidservant named Dhanakanakā, with wealth, gold, and other gifts. They proposed a stratagem to her, saying: "O fortunate lady, this Kālidāsa is swallowing our reputation. Not one among us can rival him in the arts."

“Child, you must act in such a way that the king banishes him to another country,” she said. The maidservant replied, “Having received the necklace from you, I shall perform your service; therefore, the necklace must first be given to me. Then, taking the necklace given by them, the betel-bearer reflected: “For what indeed is impossible for the wise?”

Then, after several days had passed, by chance while the king was sleeping alone, she performed services for him such as massaging his feet and, feigning sleep, closed her eyes right there. Then, perceiving that the king had become slightly awake from the movement of his feet, she said: "Friend Madanamālinī, that wicked Kālidāsa has entered the inner apartments in the guise of a maidservant and is sporting with Queen Līlādevī."

Having heard this, the king rose and said, "Taraṅgavatī, why are you awake? But she, as if distracted by sleep, did not hear him. Hearing her indistinct murmur, the king reflected: "This Taraṅgavatī, having fallen under the power of a dream while asleep, has spoken of the queen's misconduct due to the force of her latent impressions (*vāsanā*). It is even possible that he enters the inner apartments in female attire; for who indeed can truly know the conduct of women?"

Then, having reflected thus, the king on the following morning feigned a fever for himself and lay down. Having summoned Kālidāsa by means of a maidservant, and immediately after his arrival, having likewise summoned Queen Līlādevī through that same woman, he said to the queen: "My dear, I must now take my medicine. When this was said, she did the same; taking the medicine, she gave it to the king in a silver bowl and served him a soup of green gram (*mudga*). Then the king, wishing to ascertain their intentions, recited half a verse:
"How can Mudgalā, who is a serpent of speech, be devoid of husks, O Lord of Poets?
Then, even while the Queen was standing nearby, Kālidāsa spoke the second half of the verse:
"She has become free from her bodice upon union with the lover of the blind. (142)

Having heard that, the Queen, who had understood the true nature of the matter, became like Sarasvatī herself; knowing its significance, she made her face slightly smile. The King, seeing this, reflected: "In the past, she was fond of Kālidāsa, yet even now, while he stands so close to her, he has spoken thus. And she has become smiling-faced. Who knows the conduct of women?
'The leaping of a horse, the thundering of Indra, the heart of women, and the fortune of men;
drought and excessive rain—the god does not know these, much less a mortal. (143)

However, reflecting that "this Brahmin must not be killed even for such a grave offense; he is a special incarnation of Sarasvatī," [the King] said to Kālidāsa: "O Poet, you must by no means remain in our country. What need is there for much speaking? You must not utter a single word in reply. Thereupon, Kālidāsa rose up with haste, went to the house of a courtesan, and said to her: "My dear, grant me leave.
Bhoja is angry with me and has declared that I must not remain in my own country. Alas!"
Fate brings about the impossible and renders the well-ordered impossible;
indeed, it ordains those very things that a man does not even conceive of. 144.
Furthermore, it appears that this is merely the behavior of a certain group of scholars; for instance: "The combination of many things, though each of little substance, is difficult to overcome.
A rope is fashioned from blades of grass, and by means of it, even elephants are bound. (145)
Then a courtesan named Vilāsavatī said to him:
"That alone is his supreme friend wherein both pleasure and pain are reflected, like a reflection in a mirror when it is seen. (146)

“O beloved, while I am here, what need have you for the king, or what use have you for the wealth bestowed by the king? Stay happily and without fear within the inner chamber of my house. Thereupon, Kālidāsa remained in that very place for several days.

Then, when Kālidāsa had departed from the house, Līlādevī said to the king: “My Lord, there is an exceedingly close friendship between Your Majesty and the poet Kālidāsa. Why then has this improper act been committed, whereby even his staying in the country has been forbidden?”
Just as there is a gradual excellence of flavor at every successive joint starting from the tip of a sugar cane,
so too is the friendship of the virtuous, while that of the contrary is its opposite.
A protection against sorrow and enemies, a vessel for joy and confidence—who created this jewel consisting of the two syllables "mitra" (friend)? 148.

The king, having heard these words of Queen Līlā, said: "Queen, someone told me that Kālidāsa, having entered the inner apartments in the guise of a maidservant, is sporting with you. Desiring to ascertain the truth of this matter, I observed both him and you under the pretext of a simulated fever. Then, even while you were standing nearby, he spoke these words as the second half of the verse. Upon hearing them, you too laughed.

"Then, having seen all this, I—fearing the killing of a Brahmin—banished him from the country. And I do not kill you out of courtesy. Thereupon, the Goddess, overcome with laughter and filled with wonder, said: "Fearlessly, O Lord, I alone am blessed, for you, my sovereign, am my husband. Since my heart has been tasted by you, how could it go elsewhere? For even by all other women, you must be remembered during the enjoyment of their lovers."

"Aha! O King, if you depart having judged me to be either virtuous or unvirtuous, then I shall certainly die. Then the king said, "My dear, you speak the truth. Thereupon, that monarch had a serpent brought by his men; he had a heated iron ball prepared, and he strung his bow. Then the queen, having bathed and glowing with the fire of her own wifely devotion, looked at the sun and said: "O Eye of the World, you know all things.
Whether my husband be awake, dreaming, or in deep sleep—"
Only Bhoja, and no other, has been cultivated within my mind. 149.

Having said this, he then performed the three divine acts [of bathing, anointing, and adorning]. Then, while Līlāvatī was purified in the inner apartments, the king, with his head bowed in shame, spoke before her out of remorse: "O Queen, forgive me, a sinner; what can I say? Thus he lamented. From that time forward, the king neither slept nor ate, nor did he speak to anyone. Remaining with a deeply troubled mind, he lamented day and night: "What indeed is my shame? What is my courtesy? Where is my gravity?"

"Alas, alas, O poet! O crest-jewel of millions of poets, Kālidāsa! Alas, my very life-breath! Alas! Why have you been made to hear what should not be heard by this fool? Why have you been addressed with what should not be said? Thus speaking, as if asleep, as if seized by a planet, as if struck down by an illusion, he fell. Then, having regained consciousness through the water sprinkled from his beloved’s lotus-hands, he somehow beheld that very same beloved and remained there, intent on self-reproach.

Then, the assembly of King Bhoja did not shine without Kālidāsa, like a night without the lord of the stars, like the beauty of day deprived of the sun, like a woman separated from her lover, or like the Sudharmā hall bereft of Śakra. From that time forward, no one’s mouth uttered poetry; no one spoke words beautiful with wit.

Then, after some days had passed, on one occasion, beholding the orb of the full moon of the *rākā* night and seeing before him the moon-like face of Queen Līlā, he said: "The moon indeed follows the comparison of this lady’s moon-face, point for point."

And where are the playful glances of the eyes even when the moon is full? Or when is there the playfulness of speech? Having risen at dawn and performed his morning rites, the king entered the assembly hall and said to the best of the learned: "O poets, let this poetic challenge (*samasyā*) be completed. Then he recited:
"The moon follows in comparison to the smallness of this very face-moon;
the moon follows in comparison, indeed, to this face-moon."

He spoke again: "If this problem is not solved by you, you must not remain in my kingdom. Terrified, those poets returned to their own homes. Although they deliberated for a long time, the meaning did not occur to anyone. Then, having all come together, Bāṇa was sent. Having reached the assembly, he said to the king: "O Lord, I have been sent by all the learned men. Set an eight-day deadline; on the ninth day, they will solve it."

"If they do not depart from this place," [the king said]. Then the King replied, "So be it. Thereupon Bāṇa, having informed them of the King's command, returned to his own home. Eight days passed. On the night of the eighth day, when those poets had assembled, Bāṇa said: "Alas! Kālidāsa was driven out by the intoxication of youth, by the negligence of royal favor, and by a certain pride in his learning. You all are indeed equal as poets; yet in a difficult situation, he alone is the true poet."

Now that he has been expelled, what indeed was his greatness? While he remained, how could such a state as this have befallen us? Whatever intellect was employed in his expulsion, its consequences are being experienced by you yourselves.
It is said that in the enmity of an ordinary Brahmin, there may be the destruction of a lineage;
but in the enmity of one who possesses the form of Umā, there is indeed the destruction of the entire assembly of poets.

Then all the peacocks and others began to quarrel fiercely. Thereupon, having restrained them all from their brawling, they immediately said: "The deadline is fulfilled this very day; no one else has the capacity to complete the poetic fragment (*samasyā*).
In the circle of poets, as among the great warriors in battle, brilliance or the loss of brilliance occurs in a mere moment. (151)

"If it pleases you, then this very day at midnight, while the moon is shining brightly, let us depart in secret, taking our accumulated wealth. If we do not go, tomorrow the king’s servants will drive us out by force; then we shall have to depart with nothing but our bodies. Therefore, we shall go tonight at midnight. Having thus decided, they returned home, loaded their wealth onto carts drawn by oxen, and departed in the night itself.

Then Kālidāsa, staying that very night in the garden of Vilāsavatī’s residence, heard the voices of those passing on the road and sent a female servant of the courtesan. She said, “My dear, look, who are these walking along like Brahmins? Then she approached and saw them all. Having come near, she said to Kālidāsa:
“The beauty that a single royal swan imparts to a lake, That cannot be achieved by a thousand herons dwelling all around its shores. (152)

"And all those led by Bāṇa and Mayūra are fleeing; of this there is no doubt. Kālidāsa said: "My dear, quickly bring garments from the house so that I may protect the fleeing brahmins. What is manliness if it does not protect those in distress? Or what is wealth if it is not for the sake of those who seek it? What is action if it is not connected with benefit? And what indeed is life that is opposed to the virtuous? (153)

Then Kālidāsa, having assumed a charming disguise and brandishing a sword, traveled half a *krośa* further north; approaching them face-to-face and observing them all, he uttered the benediction “Victory! and inquired in the dialect of the *cāraṇas*: “O oceans of learning, you who have attained great eminence in the court of the Bhoja king, where do you wish to go together like the sages headed by Bṛhaspati? Is all well with you? And is the King well?”

“We have come from the land of Kāśī to see the Bhoja king and out of a desire for wealth. Thereupon, they all departed while making jokes. Then, one among them, having heard those words and thinking him to be a *cāraṇa* (bard), Vipaścit spoke out of curiosity: “O bard, listen! You shall certainly hear this later as well; therefore, I shall say it this very day. It is said that the King has uttered a *samasyā* (a poetic fragment) for these scholars to complete.”

Unable to complete it and fearing the wrath of the king, they departed for some other land, desiring to go elsewhere. The bard asked: "What was the poetic puzzle (*samasyā*) set by the king? Then that learned man recited: "The moon follows the face-moon of this woman, indeed, as an atom [follows] a mountain. The bard said: "This is indeed well-stated, though its meaning is hidden. Having seen the full orb of the moon, the king recited this; the second half of this verse ought to be as follows:"
"How can it be described as 'atomic' when its reflection is the very opposite of the moon?"
