Having heard this, everyone was struck with wonder. Then the wandering bard, having prostrated before them all, departed. Thereupon, they all deliberated: "Aha! This is Sarasvatī herself, come in human form for the protection of us all. This cannot be a mere mortal. Even now, nothing has been discovered by anyone. Therefore, having reached home as quickly as possible and unloading the burden from the carts, everyone must come to the royal palace tomorrow morning.

“If he does not announce it at the very moment of recitation, then we shall depart immediately. Having thus arranged it, they acted accordingly. Then, having gone to the royal assembly and beheld the king, they entered after saying, “May it be well with you. Thereupon Bāṇa said: “O King, that which is read by you, the omniscient one, only the Lord knows; for what are these wretched brahmins, who merely fill their own bellies? Nevertheless, it is said: ‘The moon follows even an atom; indeed, by this [comparison], the face is like the moon. How can one describe it as an “atom” (anu) when its likeness is a match for the moon? (154)”
"The dimness of the moon follows in comparison to this face-moon;
how can its imitation be described as the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight?"—this was the shadow [of his meaning].

The King, having understood the intention of one who had thus resolved, said: "In every way, Kālidāsa resides in a place reachable within a day's journey; and everything can be accomplished through expedients. Thereupon, he gave fifteen lakhs of gold coins to Bāṇa. Under the very pretext of providing satisfaction, the assembly of scholars was sent back to their respective homes.

When the circle of learned men had departed, the king slowly instructed the doorkeeper: "If any twice-born men should arrive, they must be brought into the inner apartments. Then, after Bāṇa had taken all his wealth and gone to his own home, some scholars said: "Alas! Bāṇa has acted improperly. For although he too has departed from the city along with us, he has taken away all the wealth. By all means, we shall inform Bhoja of Bāṇa’s true character."

“Just as no one among the learned would commit an injustice,” they said. Then, having approached the king, they beheld him. The king said to them, “The nature of this matter is already known. You must speak the truth. Thereupon, everything was reported by them. Then the king reflected, “In every way, Kālidāsa is staying within my city in the guise of a bard out of fear of me. He then commanded his bodyguards, “Ho! Let the horses be galloped away!”

Then, as they set out for the pleasure garden, the sound of kettledrums arose: "Aha! We have heard that the King is currently occupied with the worship of the gods; yet now he will go to the pleasure garden. Thus, all the soldiers, becoming agitated, followed after him in a great crowd. Then the King, mounting his horse together with those learned men, reached at night the place where the encounter with the wandering minstrels had occurred.

Then the king summoned those skilled in tracking the footprints of wandering thieves and said to them, "The footprints of someone who departed at night by this path are still visible; let them be examined. Thereupon, the king gave a hundred thousand coins to each scholar, sent them forth, and returned to his own palace. Those trackers, though searching everywhere by the king's command, remained as if bewildered, unable to find him.

Then, as the sun was hanging low, they saw a certain maidservant going toward a cobbler’s workshop carrying a single broken sandal; they were as if delighted. Seeing that sandal placed in the cobbler’s hand, they took it from her hand under a pretext, dropped it on a dust-covered path, and recognizing that very sandal as hers, they watched the maidservant as she gradually entered the courtesan’s house and surrounded her residence.

Then, in an instant, those messengers brought news of the recognition token within the range of the Bhoja king’s hearing. Thereupon, the king, together with his citizens and ministers, went on foot to Vilāsavatī’s palace. Having heard this, Kālidāsa said to Vilāsavatī: “Beloved, look at what suffering you endure for my sake! O wise Vilāsavatī, when a calamity befalls men, their true character is fully measured.
When the wind blows, no difference whatsoever appears between a heap of cotton and a mountain. (155)
On the touchstone of adversity, a person comes to know the true worth of friends, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as the depth of one's own intellect and fortitude. (156)
Just as sufferings come upon embodied beings unbidden, so too do pleasures; yet I consider that in this matter, wretchedness alone exceeds all else.

"O good poet, if you are even slightly rejected by the king, then with my word, this entire company of female slaves shall throw themselves into a blazing fire! Kālidāsa said, "My dear, you must not think so; upon seeing me, Bhoja will open his face in a smile and fall at my feet. Then, having entered the courtesan’s house, Bhoja saw Kālidāsa, embraced him with great excitement, and fell at his feet. And that king recited:
"Whether I am walking or standing still, whether I am awake or even sleeping—may my mind never, O poet, be separated from you. (158)

Having heard this, Kālidāsa stood with his face bowed down in shame. The king, raising Kālidāsa’s face, said: “O Kālidāsa, abode of the arts, if you were made to walk like a servant here on the royal road, what blame could there be for others in that matter? (159)
"I consider the playful woman to be blessed, since Kālidāsa has been bound by her own virtues, like a bird in a cage. (160)

The king wiped the tears of joy from his eyes with both hands upon seeing Kālidāsa. Then, delighted by that acquisition, the king gave one hundred thousand coins (*lakṣa*) to each of the Brahmins. Placing Kālidāsa upon his own horse, he returned to his palace accompanied by his retinue.
After some time had passed, the king once observed the twilight and said:
"The sun is falling into the ocean."
Then Bāṇa said:
"The intoxicated bee within the interiors of the lotuses.
Then the poet Maheśvara said:
“A bird in the hollow of a tree in the grove. Then Kālidāsa said:
“Slowly, slowly, the bodiless god [of love] among young women. (161)
The king, being pleased, gave him one hundred thousand [gold pieces] for each [verse]; for the fourth quarter, he gave two hundred thousand.

Once, while returning along a path in the midst of an outer garden, the king saw a certain brahmin approaching. Observing a leather water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hand and knowing him to be extremely poor, yet seeing that he was radiant with the splendor of his countenance, the king halted his horse before him and said: "O brahmin, for what purpose do you carry a leather vessel in your hand?"

That Brahmin, considering it certain that the Bhoja king was [so named] because of his handsome countenance and gentle speech, said: "O King, while Bhoja—the crest-jewel of the munificent—rules the earth, a scarcity of iron and copper has arisen. Therefore, I carry a vessel made of leather. The king asked: "While Bhoja rules, what is the cause for the absence of iron and copper? Then the Brahmin recited:
"For this illustrious King Bhoja, two things alone are very difficult to obtain: iron, from the chains of his enemies; and copper, from the plates of his edicts. (162)
Thereupon, the king, being pleased, granted a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every syllable.

Once, the gatekeeper said: "O Lord of Dhārā, a certain learned man has arrived from a distant land and stands at the gate, along with his wife and his son together with his wife. Thus, this most holy family of scholars stands at the gate. The king exclaimed: "Oh, how great is the path of Śāradā’s grace!"

At that moment, Gajendrapāla approached, bowed to the king, and said: "O Lord of the Bhojas, the sovereign of Siṃhala has sent one hundred and twenty-five lordly elephants and sixteen great jewels. Then Bāṇa said:
"The condition of elephants—whether in their own stables or in the royal palace—is like that of poets: it remains the same."
"Why is it that in every house there are these beings, adorned with royal ornaments, appearing like gnats? || 163 ||

Then the king went outside to inspect the elephants. Upon seeing that assembly of learned men, the Colapaṇḍita conceived the pride of thinking, "I am the favorite of the king," for while he was entering the interior of the royal palace, the assembly of learned men remained outside even though they had been announced by the gatekeepers. At that time, the king, perceiving the pride in his mind, had the Colapaṇḍita expelled from the courtyard of the palace.
A certain resident of the land of Kāśī named Taṇḍuladeva stood before the king after saying, "May there be well-being. The king asked him, "O wise one, where is your residence? Taṇḍuladeva replied:
"O illustrious King of Mālava, I dwell in that land where that Speech resides, which is like a sword for trees that have been stripped of their branches. (164)
The king, being pleased, gave him seven lordly elephants.
Then, a certain wise man arrived and said: "The riches of asceticism are to be attained through penance; yet even that penance does not exist [in you]."
By this means, O Bhoja, you shall come within the range of vision of the Kalpavṛkṣa.

The king gave him ten lordly elephants. Then, a certain son of a Brahmin approached making a great clamor. Thereupon, everyone was alarmed and asked, "Why do you make such a clamor? He was brought before the king's sight and questioned by him. He replied:
"O King, as I am sinking into poverty within the ocean of Your Majesty’s charity—"
For no one indeed offers a hand of support to one who bestows gifts upon an intoxicated elephant. || 166 ||
Then the king, being pleased, gave him thirty lordly elephants.
Thereupon, a certain wise man named Vilocana enters accompanied by his wife; having said "Svasti," he spoke:
"Seeing the Bhoja king giving away even his own elephants, Pārvatī [was moved]."
"Today he protects his son, whose face is like that of a lordly elephant, again and again. || 167 ||
Then the king gave him seven elephants.

Thereupon, seeing the family of the learned man standing before him at that very moment, the king said to the brahmin: "The success of great men arises from their inner strength, not from external implements."
The elderly brahmin said:
"A jar for a dwelling place, deer for attendants, birch bark for clothing, residence in the forest, and roots and such for food— one possessing qualities such as these..."

Since Agastya placed the ocean within the hollow of his lotus-like hand, it is clear that for the great, success in action depends upon their inner strength (sattva) and not upon external implements. || 168 ||
Then the king gave her sixteen jewels of great value. Thereupon, the king said to his wife, "Mother, you too recite. The queen replied:
"The chariot has but one wheel; seven horses are yoked by serpents; the path is without support; the driver is footless."
The sun reaches the end of the boundless sky day after day;
the accomplishment of great beings depends upon their inner strength, not upon external instruments. || 166 ||

The king, being pleased, gave her seventeen elephants and seven chariots. Then the king said to the Brahmin’s son, “O son of a Brahmin, you too must recite. The Brahmin’s son replied: “Laṅkā was to be conquered; the ocean was to be crossed on foot; the enemy was the descendant of Pulastya; and the allies in the field of battle were monkeys.
Yet this mortal, fighting on foot, destroyed the entire race of Rākṣasas.”
The accomplishment of the task of the great depends upon the being, not upon the instrument.

The king, being pleased, gave eighteen lordly elephants to the daughter of the Brahmin. Then, beholding his son’s daughter-in-law—whose every limb and member was delicate, charming, and adorned; who appeared like a personification of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) born from a Campaka creeper, a slender stalk of beauty—the king thought in his heart, “Surely she is some playful manifestation of Sarasvatī,” and after bowing, he said: “Mother, you too must grant me a blessing. The Brahmin’s daughter-in-law replied: “O King, listen. The bow is made of flowers, and the bowstring consists of bees for those with tremulous eyes.”
The corner of an eye is an arrow; even the cold-rayed moon is a friend, though its nature is inert;
and Cupid himself is bodiless—yet he agitates the entire world.
Success for the great depends upon their inner strength, not upon external instruments. || 171 ||

The king, filled with wonder, took all the ornaments of Queen Līlādevī and gave them to her; he also bestowed upon her priceless gold, pearls, and emeralds. Then, on one occasion, a poet named Sīmanta said:
"O Sun, withdraw your path and abandon your harsh splendor!"

"O glorious Vindhya mountain, be gracious; be merciful and come near at once!"—thus do your enemies, O glorious Bhoja, speak and faint every day upon seeing their beloved fleeing far away, exhausted by her flight. 172.

At that very moment, a certain goldsmith approached and presented a golden vessel adorned with rubies at its edges before the king. Then the king said to the court poet Sīmantaka: "O good poet, this vessel displays a certain splendor. Thereupon the poet replied: "O Lord of the Earth, the Sun, defeated by your majesty, serves you alone, O King, under the pretext of being this golden vessel. (13)

Thereupon, the king, being pleased, filled that very bowl with pearls and gave it to him. Once, while the king was out hunting, he saw a boar fleeing ahead and, being alone, reached the edge of a distant forest. There, seeing a certain eminent brahmin, he said, "Brahmin, where are you going? The brahmin replied, "To Dhārānagara."
Bhoja: "For what purpose?
The Brahmin: "To see Bhoja, out of a desire for wealth. He gives it to a scholar; I, too, do not beg from a fool.
Bhoja: "O Brahmin, in that case, you must be either a learned man or a poet."
The Brahmin: O illustrious one, I am a poet.
Bhoja: Then recite something. The Brahmin: No one knows the path of my verses except Bhoja.
The King: I too possess knowledge of the speech of the immortals; the King is well-disposed toward me, and I shall cause your virtues to be heard. Display some skill in the arts.
The Brahmin: What shall I describe?
The King: Describe these *kalamā* rice grains.

The Brahmin said: “The *kalamā* rice stalks, bent low by ripeness, their fragrant white lilies (*kalhāra*) sniffed at the base of their roots, and their heads shaken by the breeze, generally evoke praise for their sweet scent. (174)

The king removed all his ornaments and gave them to him. Then, on one occasion, the potter’s wife came to the royal palace and said to the gatekeeper: “Gatekeeper, the king must be seen. He asked, “What business do you have with the king? She replied, “I will not tell it to you; I shall speak it only in the presence of the monarch. Having entered the assembly hall, he said, “Your Majesty, a certain beloved of a potter desires an audience with the king, yet she does not state her business before me.”
"She will speak before you. The king said, "Let her enter. She came forward, bowed, and said:
"My lord, a treasure was discovered by my husband while digging for earth;
he remains right there looking at it, and I have come to inform you. (175)

The king was filled with wonder and had the treasure-jar brought. As soon as the king opened its lid and looked within, he beheld the circle of light radiating from the jewels contained inside and asked the potter, "What is this, potter? He replied:
"Beholding the moon-like king who has descended to the surface of the earth, I believe the stars have come here in the guise of this series of gems. (176)
Having heard this extraordinary verse from the mouth of the potter, the king was filled with wonder and gave him everything.

Then, on one occasion, the king was wandering alone at night, observing the activities throughout the city and listening to the voices of the citizens. At that time, in a certain merchant’s house, a merchant said to his beloved wife: "My dear, although this king is devoted to giving only a little, he aspires to the reputation for generosity of Vikramārka, the lord of the city of Ujjayinī. Can that be attained by Bhoja? Bhoja has been brought to greatness by certain poets such as Mayūra, who are solely intent on composing hymns of praise; yet, my dear, Bhoja remains merely Bhoja. Listen, my dear."

If a dog, its shoulder-blade made bristly with tied-on artificial manes, were mounted upon the position of the lion, the enemy of deer, how could it produce the roar of the lord of beasts, who is intent on splitting the temples of rutting elephants? (177)

Having heard this, the king reflected, "He speaks the truth indeed. Then he heard him speaking again and again: "Only one in distress is a worthy recipient; the mere utterance of 'Give! is no mark of wisdom.
To give only when the occasion arises—O Vikramārka, how can your generosity be sufficiently praised? (178)
O Vikramārka, you have granted eight hundred prosperous villages to a son of a Brahmin who was a petitioner; O Bhoja, where is your greatness? (179)
"Even a potter attains the greatness of Prajāpati if your valor finds its footing even among the Bhojas. (180)

The king thought, "Every person in the world speaks the truth fearlessly within their own home. Whether by me or by another, the fame of Vikramārka can never be attained. Then, one day, a certain poet arrived at the palace gate and said, "The king must be seen. He was then ushered in, and after saying "Svasti" to the king, he sat down by the king's command and recited:
"Among poets, among debaters, among serpents, among embodied beings, among the wealthy, and among those who benefit the virtuous—"
On this earth, among those who possess wealth, those who wield the bow, and even those whose wealth is the Dharma, there is no king equal to Bhoja. || 181 ||
The king gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces], and having removed all his ornaments, he gave him that horse as well.

Then, once while the king was proceeding to a pleasure garden, he saw on the road a certain woman with beautiful eyes wearing soiled garments, her lotus-face scorched by the rays of the exceedingly hot sun; looking at her with his own eyes, he asked, "Who are you, daughter?
And she, recognizing King Bhoja by the splendor of his face, spoke joyfully:
"O King," [said] the hunter's wife;
and the king, filled with joy, asked her because of the continuity of her clever composition, "What is this in your hand?"
She said, “A burden. The king asked, “Is it emaciated?
She replied, “I speak of that which is innate, O King, if you will listen with respect.”
On the banks of the river that is the beloved of your enemies, the wives of the Siddhas sing;
blinded by those songs, the deer do not graze on grass, and the weak birds do not seek prey.
The king gave her a hundred thousand coins for every syllable.
Then, having returned home, he sat by the window. Seeing Bhoja seated there, someone standing on the royal road said: "O Lord, ruler of the entire earth, listen!
Here comes the bridge, its banks shattered by the waters from this side and that."
The earth is difficult to traverse, and this mountain is thick with mire from the heavy snow;
now that the ritual lustration of elephants and horses has been completed,
I know not by what path you and your enemies have departed.

The gratified Bhoja gave five elephants of his lineage to him even as he stood upon the road. Once, the king, overcome by a passion for hunting, mounted his horse and set forth. Then, seeing a man who had just crossed a river with firewood placed upon his head, and recognizing him by his appearance to be a Brahmin, the king quickly questioned him.
"How deep is the water, O Brahmin?
He replied, "It reaches up to the knees, O Lord of Men.
Astonished, the king said, "How can you be in such a state?"
He said: "Not all people are like you. || 185 ||

Out of curiosity, the king said, "Learned sir, ask the treasurer; by my word he will give you a hundred thousand. Thereupon, the learned man cast his staff upon the ground, went to the treasurer, and said, "I have been sent by the Great King."

"Let a hundred thousand be given to me. Then, laughing, he said: "O Brahmin, your form does not merit a hundred thousand. Thereupon, the despondent man went to the king and said: "Your Majesty, he laughs again; he will not give it. Out of curiosity, the king said: "Ask for two hundred thousand; he will give them. Returning once more, the Brahmin said: "The king has said that two hundred thousand should be given. He laughed yet again.

The Brahmin approached the Bhoja king once more and said, "That most wicked man laughs at me and does not grant me [the gift]. Then, the illustrious King Bhoja—the treasure-house of playfulness who ruled the earth—being curious, said: "Brahmin, ask for three hundred thousand; he will certainly give them. He returned and said, "The king is having three hundred thousand granted to me. [Upon hearing this,] the man laughed again. Thereupon, the enraged Brahmin returned once more and said: "O Lord, he simply does not grant it.
O King, while you rain gold-streams everywhere, he alone remains obstinate."
While I am covered by the parasol of misfortune, not even drops [of rain] fall upon me.
When the rain-cloud pours down, all trees put forth new shoots;
yet for us, the *arka* trees, there is doubt even regarding our previous leaves. (187)
One aspect of this thing is supreme, while another aspect is base;
by the ever-shining light, the perpetual darkness is constantly driven away. || 188 ||
Then the king said:
"O twice-born one, do not be angry; at my word, go to the treasury official and take for yourself three hundred thousand [gold pieces] and ten lordly elephants. (189)
Then he dispatches a bodyguard. Thereupon, the treasurer writes in the legal document:

"One hundred thousand, another hundred thousand, and yet another hundred thousand, along with ten rutting elephants, were given by Bhoja when he was pleased by [the boy’s] speech reaching up to his knees. (190)
Then, while King Śrī Bhoja was seated upon his throne, the doorkeeper approached and said:

“O King, a certain poet named Śukadeva, tormented by poverty, stands at the gate. Bāṇa said to the king: “O best of scholars, O excellent poet, do you know him? Bāṇa—[intending] that only Kālidāsa, and no one else, possessed the capacity to recognize Śukadeva—said: “O King, O excellent poet, friend Kālidāsa, do you know the poet Śukadeva? Kālidāsa replied: “O Lord, I know two excellent poets on this entire earth.”
“Bhavabhūti, Śuka, and this Vālmīki—these three [are the masters] among them.
Then Sītā, who is honored by the assembly of the learned, said:
“What do crows not do? They utter their croaking here and there.”
Only the parrot, cherished in the king's hand, speaks excellently. || 192 ||
Then the peacock said:
"A man who speaks something unasked in the assembly of a king receives not only dishonor, but also ridicule. (193)
"O King, nevertheless it is said:
'What is the assembly? What is the poet's knowledge? Who are the connoisseurs and who are the poets?
O Bhoja, what indeed is your gift, by which that parrot is satisfied? (194)"

"Nevertheless, Śukadeva, having arrived at the palace gate, must certainly be brought into the assembly hall. Then the king, having heard of Śukadeva’s literary prowess, became a vessel for both joy and sorrow. He felt joy because he beheld a great poet; yet he felt sorrow, wondering what indeed could be given to this crest-jewel among the millions of true poets. "Very well. Gatekeeper, let him enter. Then, seeing Śukadeva approaching, the king rose from his throne.

All the scholars, having bowed with humility to Śukadeva, invited him to be seated. The king, for his part, seated him upon the throne and sat down himself by his command. Then Śukadeva said: "O King, Lord of Dhārā, it is the fortune of the gift-bestowing King Vikrama that serves you alone. O King, the Lord of Mālava alone is blessed, and no other monarchs; for poets such as Kālidāsa dwell at your court like birds bound by strings. Then he recited:
"Out of fear of Bhoja’s majesty, the Sun attained the status of a friend [to Bhoja]."
The Aurva fire assumes the state of the Vāḍava, and the lightning has attained momentariness. || 195 ||
The king said, "Stay, O good poet; no further verse is to be recited:
'Bhoja, being well-pleased, gave to the parrot a divine golden pitcher filled with rubies, as well as four hundred elephants. (196)

Having thus written on the certificate of merit and bestowed everything, the treasurer dispatched Śuka. The king was delighted to learn that Śuka had departed for his own country, and the assembly was likewise satisfied.
On another occasion, during the rainy season, a certain poet named Vāsudeva arrived and saw the king. The king said, "O good poet, recite a poem on the rain-cloud. Thereupon, the poet spoke:

“Neither by wish-fulfilling gems, nor by Kalpa-trees, nor by the Kāmadhenu and others, nor even by the gods who are devoted to helping others—neither by the gross nor by the subtle—is the world sustained.
I believe it is only through you, O cloud-bodied one, the leader who now bears the burden, sprinkling that parched earth incessantly with loads of water, that the world lives. || 197 ||
The king gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces].
Once, observing that the king was constantly giving away wealth, the chief minister, unable to speak [openly], inscribed clear letters on the wall of the king’s bedchamber:
“One should save wealth for times of misfortune.”
The king, rising from his bed and walking along, saw those letters on the wall and himself wrote the second line: "Whence can misfortunes come to the illustrious?
On the following day, the minister, seeing the second line written, himself wrote the third:
"If that fortune has departed..."
On the following day, the king wrote the fourth line: “Accumulated wealth perishes. || 198 ||

Then the chief minister fell at the king’s feet and said, “Your Majesty, this offense of mine must be forgiven. Once, thinking that the Lord of Dhārā was sleeping on the upper floor of the palace, a certain thief of a Brahmin broke through the wall and entered the royal treasury. Having stolen many various jewels, such as lapis lazuli and the like, and regarding them as debts to be paid in the next world, he became filled with world-weariness right there and reflected:
‘Those who are deformed, those with leprosy, the blind, the lame, and the poor—’”
Embodied beings experience the fruit of the evil they have previously accumulated. || 199 ||

Then, at the end of his sleep, the king, reclining upon his celestial couch, beheld his lovely retinue adorned with various jeweled bracelets; and reflecting upon his abundance of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, he was satisfied by the pleasures of sovereignty and, out of an overflow of joy, said: "Captivating young women, well-disposed friends, noble kinsmen, and servants whose speech is filled with affection—"
"The herds of elephants leap and the horses gallop"—these three lines were spoken by the king. When the fourth line did not emerge from the king's mouth, the thief heard it and completed it:
"When the eyes are closed, there is nothing at all. (200)

Then the king, having knotted his own bracelet, saw the thief and gave it to him. Thereupon, the thief took the hero’s bracelet, went to the house of a Brahmin, woke the sleeping Brahmin, gave it to him, and said: "O Brahmin, this king’s bracelet is of great value; it must not be sold for a small price. Then the Brahmin, having sold it in the marketplace, acquired divine ornaments and fine silk garments.

Then some royal officers, suspecting him to be a thief, reported him to the king. He was led into the presence of the king. The king asked, "O wearer of the *viṭa*-garment, you do not even possess a cloth. From where did these divine earrings, ornaments, and fine silk garments come this very morning? The Brahmin replied:
"In this [place], it was as if dead due to frogs dwelling in hollows, as if fainted by tortoises and *pāṭhīna* fish from repeatedly wallowing on the broad surface of the mud."
Into that dried-up lake came an unseasonal cloud, performing such a feat that herds of wild elephants, submerged up to their trunks, drank the water. || 201 ||
The king, being pleased, recognized that the hero’s bracelet had been given by the thief and bestowed upon him a hundred thousand [gold pieces] himself.
On another occasion, a certain lord of poets named Viṣṇu arrived at the royal gate; having been ushered in by them, he beheld the king and, after pronouncing a blessing, said:
"O Lord of Dhārā, one who is eager to count the great Indra-like kings of the earth..."
While counting you, the Creator drew a line in the sky with a piece of chalk;

that very line became this river of the gods (the Ganges). However, due to the absence of any mountain equal to you, it has left the surface of the earth and remains here as this snowy mountain (the Himalayas).

Having heard the extraordinary verse, the king pondered, "What should be given? At that moment, having heard his peerless poetic skill, the face of the poet named Somanātha became pale with envy. Then, out of malice, he said to the king: "Your Majesty, this man is indeed a fine poet; however, he has never before beheld a royal court, for he is an ocean of poverty.
He does not even possess a worn-out loincloth. Thereupon the king said to Somanātha:
"If his verses are faultless, what loss is there to one who is without a protector?"
If a sugarcane stalk placed under the armpit of a monk were to become sapless, [what could be done]? || 203 ||

Then, having distributed betel to everyone, the king rose from the assembly. Thereupon, they all said to one another, "Today, having heard the poetry of Viṣṇukavi, Somanātha has displayed his true malice. Then the circle of scholars rose. Next, Viṣṇukavi wrote a verse on a leaf, placed it in the hand of the poet Somanātha, and after bowing, began to depart. "May you alone rejoice for a long time in this assembly! Then the poet Somanātha read it: [The verse follows] [The verse ends with: "O King, may you live long; O Goddess Sarasvatī, may you be victorious! Upon hearing this, the entire assembly was filled with wonder. Then the king said, "What is this? Somanātha replied, "This is the work of Viṣṇukavi. The king then asked, "Where is he? Somanātha said, "He has gone. The king then said, "Bring him back. Somanātha replied, "He will not come. The king then said, "If he does not come, I shall punish you. Somanātha said, "I am not afraid of punishment. The king then said, "If you are not afraid of punishment, then show me that verse. Somanātha then showed it. The king then said, "Is this yours? Somanātha said, "No, it is not mine. The king then said, "If it is not yours, then who wrote it? Somanātha said, "Viṣṇukavi wrote it. The king then said, "If Viṣṇukavi wrote it, then why did you give it to me? Somanātha said, "I gave it to you because I wished to hear it read. The king then said, "If you wish to hear it read, then read it yourself. Somanātha then read it. Upon hearing it, the king was filled with great joy. He then said, "This is indeed the work of Viṣṇukavi. Then he summoned Viṣṇukavi and honored him greatly. Thus, by the grace of the goddess Sarasvatī, Viṣṇukavi became famous throughout the world as a poet. ||| Thus ends the story of Viṣṇukavi. ||| [End of text]

"Alas! While these trees are being devoured by forest fires fanned by the youthful winds, O cloud, if you do not release water, then do not release it; but why, O merciless one, do you hurl your thunderbolt again? (204)

Then the poet Somanātha gave away all his silk garments, wealth, gold, and his abundance of horses and other possessions, leaving nothing but his wife’s clothing. Thereupon, as the king was traveling along, intent on the pleasures of the hunt, he beheld Viṣṇukavi and thought: “I have not even provided him with food; disregarding me, he will go toward his own country full of wealth. I shall ask him: ‘Viṣṇukavi, from where has this wealth been obtained? The poet replied:
“O King of kings, O Lord, by Somanātha, who was a mendicant at your palace—”
Today, I, who am most worthy of pity, have become like a wish-fulfilling tree for you. || 205 ||

The king gave one hundred thousand gold pieces for each syllable of the verse he had previously heard in the assembly. He then gave as much as had been given by Somanātha back to Somanātha himself. Somanātha said:
"Whence are the sprouts, where are the flowers, and likewise where are the fruits of the forest creepers?
For when this cloud, out of causeless compassion, does not pour forth its waters here [upon us], [what hope is there]? (206)

Then Viṣṇukavi was pleased by King Somanāthadatta and Datta. At that time, Sīmantakavi said: “Śeṣa bears the series of worlds resting upon the surface of his hoods; he, in turn, is always supported in the center on the back of the Lord of Tortoises.”
Even him, the ocean respectfully made subject to its lap; alas, the manifestations of the greatness of the great are indeed boundless! (207)

Once, a servant approached the king on the roof of the palace and said: "Your Majesty, whatever wealth exists in all the treasuries has been given by Your Majesty to the poets; however, not even a fraction of a coin remains in the treasury house. A certain poet stands at the gate every day."

"It must be announced by the chief minister in the presence of Your Majesty that henceforth no poet or scholar whatsoever shall be received by the King. Although the King knew that everything in the treasury had already been given away, he said: "Today, let the poet standing at the gate be admitted. Then the scholar approached, saying "Svasti," and spoke:
"In the supportless sky, for a long time the cātaka bird has sat with its upturned beak extended toward you;
let alone the showers from the clouds, even your sweet sound has not been heard by him."

Having heard this, the king thought, "Fie upon life, that learned men and poets should come to my door and suffer want! He then removed all his ornaments and gave them to that brahmin. Thereafter, the king summoned the treasurer and said, "Treasurer, among the treasuries belonging to King Muñja as well as those of my ancestors, where are the jars filled with jewels? Then, the poet Mucukunda arrived from the land of Kashmir; having said, "May there be welfare," he spoke:
"O Bhoja, as if out of fear of sinking into the ocean of your fame..."
Under the guise of the orbs of the sun and moon, the sky bears two jars. || 209 ||
The king gave him a hundred thousand coins for every single syllable. Again the poet said:
"O generous cloud, not even as many drops of water have been released by you as there have been tears shed by the cātaka birds. (210)
Then that king gave him even a hundred thoroughbred horses. Thereupon the treasurer wrote:
"To the poet Mucukunda, he gave a hundred noble steeds;
though he had already bestowed a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], the Bhoja king was asked for more by him. (211)
Then the king, having sent everyone back to their quarters, entered within. Thereupon, the queen’s fly-whisk bearer said:
“O King, lamp of the Muñja dynasty, crest-jewel of all sovereigns, it is indeed fitting for you to move about even at night under this wondrous gem-studded parasol.”
Let not the moon be bowed down with shame by the sight of your face;
let not this venerable Arundhatī become a vessel for ill-repute.
The king gave her a hundred thousand coins for every single syllable.
On another occasion, a poet named Gopāla arrived from the city of Kuṇḍina and, after offering his greetings, said:
"O Bhoja, the two things that have emerged from your mind are like mere blades of grass."
In his anger he was an army of adversaries; in his grace, a heap of gold. || 213 ||

Even upon hearing it, the king was pleased but would not grant it; he remained engaged in consultation with his royal officers. Then the poet thought, "Has the king not heard [the verse]? Then, observing the king to be indeed uplifted in an instant, the poet said:
"O Cloud, just as you have risen high, O steadfast one, I believe you will surely act so as to create a lake equal to the Ocean of Milk that pervades all directions."

But this school of fish and other creatures, distressed by the heat of summer and having you as their sole refuge, cannot endure it even for a moment; therefore, let it rain for at least that long. 214.

The king, having understood the poet’s heart, said, “O Gopālaka, you are utterly consumed by the fire of poverty,” and gave him sixteen priceless jewels and sixteen lordly elephants. Once, while wandering through the city of Dhārā, the king saw two men fast asleep in a certain temple of Śiva. One of them, whose sleep had passed, said: “Oh, who are you that lies sleeping so close to my bed? Are you awake or not? Then the other replied: “O Brahmin, I bow to you.”

"I too am the son of a Brahmin. Seeing you lying here on the first night and, while the lamp was burning, recognizing you as a Brahmin by your water-pot, sacred thread, and other signs, I fell asleep right near your bedding. Now, having heard your voice, I have awakened. The first one said: "Child, if you are devoted [to me], then may you live long!"

"Tell me, from where have you come, what is your name, and what is your business here? The second one replied: "O Brahmin, my name is Bhāskara. My residence is on the shore of the western ocean, near the holy site of Prabhāsa. There, the generosity of Bhoja has been extolled by many. Therefore, I have come to request [a gift]. Since you are like a father to me due to your seniority, please tell me of your own background. He said: "My child, my name is Śākalya."

“I am coming from the city of Mayaśilā toward Bhoja out of a desire for wealth. My child, even though you have not spoken of it, I know what kind of suffering you endure; tell me what it is. Then Bhāskara said: “Father, what can I say of my suffering?

My children, emaciated by hunger, lie like corpses with their intellects utterly dulled; and my kinsmen are smeared with the lac-residue from broken, rattling drums. Yet none of these troubles afflict me as much as this.”
When the neighbor's housewife asked for a needle, she, pretending to be angry, made a coquettish smile in order to have her own torn garment mended. || 215 ||
Having heard this, the king removed all his ornaments and, giving them to him, said: "Bhāskara, these children of yours are suffering greatly. Depart for your country at once. Then Śākalya said:
"The earth has been raised up, the host of enemies crushed, and the royal fortune of King Bali has been embraced by the powerful one."
"What this youth accomplished in a single lifetime, the Ancient Puruṣa performed over the course of three births. || 216 ||
Then the king gave three hundred thousand [gold pieces] to Śākalya.

On another occasion, while the king was wandering about out of a passion for hunting, a certain poet spoke with the hope of wealth, even though a doe had been brought before him and pierced by his arrow:

"O illustrious Bhoja, although you have gone out on the hunt, although the bow has been suddenly strung, although it has been drawn back to your ear, although the arrow has slipped from your grip, and although it has struck its mark—"
"Neither fleeing from her place, nor moving, nor trembling, nor leaping—by the hope that 'this desire will bring my beloved under my control,' the doe remains thus. ||217||
The king granted him three hundred thousand [gold pieces].

On another occasion, while King Śrībhoja was seated upon his throne, the doorkeeper approached and said, "Your Majesty, a certain wise old Brahmin woman residing on the banks of the Jāhnavī stands at the gate.
The king replied, "Let her enter. Then, as she was entering, she bowed to the king; he said to her, "Live long! and she spoke.
"Unprecedented is this fire of Bhoja’s majesty that blazes within the mountain fortresses;
once it has entered, grass grows in the courtyards of the houses of the enemy kings. (218)
The king presents her with a jar filled with jewels. Then the treasurer writes:
"A jar filled with gold and gems was given by Bhoja to the elderly woman in the royal assembly, as he was pleased by her praise of his majesty. (219)

On another occasion, a certain thief who had arrived from a distant land said to the king: "O King, in the land of Siṃhala, I saw a princess at a temple of Cāmuṇḍā; having heard many times of the greatness of the god of the Mālava country, she asked me, 'Do you also speak of him? I then described the virtues of the god to her. Out of extreme satisfaction, she gave me an incomparable piece of sandalwood from the heart of a tree and returned to her place. Accept this, which was obtained through my description of the god's virtues."

"By the weight of this spreading fragrance, even the bees and serpents are drawn here. The king, pleased by this, gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Then the poet Dāmodara, under that pretext, praised the king:
"O illustrious Sandalwood-tree, there are many such trees in the forest whose beauty consists primarily of flowers, while their fragrance merely dwells within them."
That fragrance of excellent quality which was manifested by you, renowned for your pure and celebrated nature through that well-executed work part by part— here it is seen in this *kāsī* flower.
The king, perceiving it to be praise of himself, gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces].
Then the gatekeeper arrived and said, “Your Majesty, a certain female architect is standing at the gate. The king said, “Let her enter. She then approached, prostrated before the king, and said:
“What is so wonderful here that Bali, whose abode is the netherworld (pātāla), has been cast below?”
It is a marvel that even the wish-fulfilling tree, though dwelling in heaven, has been surpassed by you.
The king gave her a hundred thousand coins for every single syllable.
Then, once, while exhausted from hunting, the king was sitting beneath a mango tree somewhere. There, a poet named Mallinātha approached and said:
“How many trees are there not in the forest, with their hundreds upon hundreds of spreading branches?”
The trees are sparse, their leaves crushed by swarms of bees clustering together in the heavy fragrance.
Then the king gave him a golden bracelet.

While the king was still seated there, a certain learned man approached, said "Svasti," and spoke: "O King, beginning from the land of Kāśī, I have been wandering on a pilgrimage through various holy sites, my strength exhausted. The king replied, "I have achieved my purpose by the sight of holy men such as yourself. He said, "We are practitioners of mantras. The king said, "Everything is possible among Brahmins. The king spoke again: "O Brahmin, just as the attainment of results in the next world comes through the science of mantras, so too—"

"Is there anything even in this world? The Brahmin replied: "O King, it is universally known that the acquisition of knowledge comes from the propitiation of the feet of Sarasvatī; however, the acquisition of wealth depends upon fortune.
Indeed, virtues are merely virtues; virtues alone are not the causes of prosperity.
For it is fortunes themselves that bring about the accumulation of wealth. (223)

"Your Majesty, it is the qualities of learning alone that serve as the foundation for people in this world, and not mere wealth. Your Majesty, when the collection of virtues depends upon oneself, the lack of virtue is indeed a matter of reproach;
but when riches depend upon destiny, what blame can there possibly be for men? (224)

"Your Majesty, through the propitiation of mantras, one's power shall become unimpeded. Your Majesty, for one who possesses such curiosity, upon whose head I place my hand, he shall have the expansion of his knowledge proceeding without obstacle through the grace of Sarasvatī. The king said, "O Sumati, the power of the deity is great. Then the king, having summoned a certain maidservant, said to the Brahmin: "O best of the twice-born, place your hand upon the head of this courtesan."

The Brahmin placed his hand upon her head and said to her, “O Queen, speak whatever Your Majesty commands. Then the maidservant said, “O King, today I perceive the entirety of all literature as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of my hand. O King, command me; what shall I describe? Thereupon, the king, looking at the sword before him, said, “Describe this sword for me. The maidservant replied:
“O Lord of Men, it is a wonder that while this sword of yours rains down [water] like a cloud, the eyes of the wives of your enemies rain down tears.”
In battle, his sword, which never fails to strike its mark,
brings poverty upon his rival kings.
The king gave her five priceless jeweled jars.
Then, at that very moment, five poets arrived from somewhere. Observing the king with a somewhat dejected countenance, the poet Maheśvara spoke through the guise of a tree:
"Were you born at a crossroads? You possess a dense shade; what is the use of that shade?"

O noble tree, if you are covered with foliage, what of it? If you are laden with fruit, what of it? If you are full of fruit, what of it? If you are bent low, what of it? Endure now for a long time the pulling, shaking, twisting, and breaking of your branches and tips by the people, caused solely by their own wicked deeds. (226)

Then the king gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Thereupon those excellent brahmins, having uttered their respective benedictions, sat down upon the blankets in due order by the king’s command and performed the auspicious rites. Then one of them recited:
"May the tortoise sport in the waters of the subterranean Gaṅgā; may the primordial boar take hold of the musta-grass growing on its banks; may the lord of serpents relax his circle of hoods;
may the elephants of the quarters engage in the act of devouring lotus stalks; and may the lords of mountains [behold the rising sun]."
"O Lord Bhoja, let all move about at their own will while you bear the goddess Earth."
The king was amazed and gave him a hundred horses. Then the treasurer wrote:
"In the pleasure garden, a hundred horses swift as thought were bestowed by the lord of men upon Kāmadeva beneath a mango tree. (228)

Then, at one time, Bhoja reflected: "There is no one as generous as I. Having perceived his pride, the chief minister showed Bhoja a document of merit (*puṇyapatra*) belonging to Vikramārka. Bhoja saw a certain passage in that document. It was as follows: Vikramārka, once thirsty, said:
"It is as clear as the heart of a virtuous man, lighter than the words of the distressed, as cooling as the embrace of a son, and likewise as sweet as the babbling of a child."
Let water be brought, made fragrant with elā, uśīra, lavaṅga, sandalwood, shining karpūra, kastūrī, jātī, pāṭali, and ketakī. || 229 ||
Then the King of Magadha said:
"The lotus of your face is the constant abode of Sarasvatī; your lower lip is indeed the Śoṇa river; your right arm is the ocean, capable of evoking the memory of Rāma’s prowess."
"O King, these armies constantly flank you and never leave you; tell me, how could a desire for water have arisen in your mind when it is so pure? (230)
Then Vikramārka said: "For instance— 'Eighty million gold pieces, ninety-three *tulās* of pearls,
fifty elephants intoxicated by the scent of honey and agitated by rage;'"
"Ten thousand horses skilled in various maneuvers and a hundred courtesans have been given as a dowry by King Pāṇḍya; let this be presented to the bard. (231)

Then Bhoja, having witnessed from the very beginning the wondrous deeds of Vikramārka, abandoned his pride. Later, once while wandering at night in the city of Dhārā, the king saw a certain Brahmin shivering with cold in a temple and reciting as follows:

"O King, for me who am enveloped by the cold like the waters of the month of Māgha, sinking in the ocean of anxiety, whose digestive fire is extinguished, whose lips are chapped, who am blowing [to warm myself], and whose belly is emaciated by hunger—"
Sleep, like some beloved woman slighted, has abandoned us and gone far away; yet the night does not diminish for us, as if the Goddess of Fortune had been bestowed upon a worthy recipient. || 232 ||
Having heard this, the king summoned him in the morning and asked, "O Brahmin, how was that terrible burden of cold endured by you last night? The Brahmin replied:
"Jānu [the knee] at night, Bhānu [the sun] by day, and Kṛśānu [fire] during the two twilights—thus was the cold passed by me through Jānu, Bhānu, and Kṛśānu. (233)
The king gave him three golden jars. Then the poet praised the king:

"Having taken upon yourself the burden of existence, you—whose life is enriched by the wealth of great renunciation—have liberated Bali, Karṇa, and others, whose deeds were protected by their own fame. (234)
The king gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces].

Once, the gardener of the pleasure grove arrived and placed a single stalk of sugarcane before the king; the king took it in his hand. Then, the poet Mayūra, keeping in mind the contempt shown toward him by the king due to their extreme familiarity, spoke under the pretext of the sugarcane:
"You are beautiful, you are eternally sweet, and you are full of flavor."
Moreover, you are the peerless bow of the five-arrowed god of love;
yet for you, the sugarcane possesses everything except for one supreme quality: that once consumed, it gradually attains a state of flavorlessness.

Having understood the poet's heart, the king honored the peacock. Then, one night, while enjoying himself upon the palace roof, the king beheld the moon and said: "As for this which displays the grace of a water-lily bud within the moon, people call it a 'hare' (śaśaka), but not so for me."
Then, having entered the interior of the palace on the ground floor below, a certain thief said:
"I, however, consider the moon to have its body marked by the specks of scars from the falling meteors of the side-glances of young women overcome by separation from their lovers. (236)

Having heard this, the king said, "O illustrious one, who are you that stays here in the middle of the treasury at midnight? He replied, "Your Majesty, grant us safety. The king said, "So be it. Then the thief bowed to the king and related his own story. Pleased, the king gave ten crores of gold and intoxicated lordly elephants to the thief. Thereupon, the treasurer wrote in the register of merit:
"The Lord, being gratified, granted these to this thief—who had conquered the fear of death—for the sake of [erecting] two upper footprints."
Ten crores of gold pieces, ten mountains with peaks shattered by his tusks, and even eight lordly elephants whose rutting cries attracted swarms of bees; || 237 ||

Then, on one occasion, the gatekeeper approached and said, “Your Majesty, a learned man who possesses nothing but a loincloth is standing at the door. The king said, “Let him enter. When the poet had entered and beheld Bhoja, he thought, “Today my poverty shall be destroyed,” and being filled with joy, he shed tears of gladness. Seeing him, the king asked, “Poet, why do you weep? Then the poet replied, “O King, listen to the state of my household:
Hearing the loud sound of parched grain on the road, my wife, her face downcast, has carefully covered the ears of our child.”
Since my means of remedy have failed and my eyes are filled with many tears for what you did not do, you alone are fit to extract that dart from within me. || 238 ||
The king, exclaiming "Śiva, Śiva! Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa!", gave a hundred thousand for each syllable and said: "O good poet, go home quickly; your wife has become distressed.

Later, once, the king, exhausted from hunting, sat resting in the shade of a certain great tree. There, a poet named Śāmbhavadeva approached and addressed the king through the metaphor of the tree: "By its fragrances, the winds [are pleased]; by the splendor of its young shoots, the deer; and by its bark, the ascetics..."
By your very flowers, the bees; by your fruits, the birds; and by your shade, those distressed by the heat;
and by your trunks, the scent-elephants—all have been made successful. Therefore, you are capable of benefiting the entire world, while other trees have their misfortunes averted only by you.
Furthermore:

Even when its merits are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears; and even before its fragrance is perceived, a garland of *mālatī* flowers captivates the eye. (240)
Delighted by those two verses, the king gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every syllable.
On another occasion, Śrī Bhoja went to the temple of Śiva to pay homage to the illustrious Maheśvara. Then, a certain Brāhmaṇa said to the king in the presence of Śiva:
"O King, half of Śiva was taken away by the enemy of the Dānavas, and half by Girijā."
Thus, O Lord, upon the disappearance of the Destroyer of Tripura from the surface of the earth,
the Ganges has reached the ocean, the sky the crescent moon, the lord of serpents the surface of the earth,
and you have attained omniscience and sovereignty; but for me, there is only the wandering for alms.
The king gave him a hundred thousand coins.
Then, on one occasion, the doorkeeper arrived and said, “Your Majesty, a certain scholar stands at the gate. The king said, “Let him enter. Thereupon the scholar entered and recited:
“Whomever your affectionate gaze favors for even a moment...”
O lord of men, poverty quickly abandons him as if out of envy.
The king gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Again the poet recites:
Some have their roots entangled in the soil; some, moreover, possess connection with the trunk; some have attained shade; others even reach the base of the branches;
some hold blossoms in their hands; and still others are merely vessels for fragrance.
But alas, the foolish do not even venture to look at the fruit of the Vāgvallī creeper! || 243 ||
Having heard this, Bāṇa said:
"Indeed, the concealed flavor of nectar, jaggery, honey, molasses,
and milk sometimes attains even greater distaste through over-familiarity."
Whether upon the bimba-like lips of a beloved or even in the eloquent speech of a charming poet, there flashes forth some boundless and incomparable aesthetic flavor (rasa) that is a fresh delight.
Then the king gave him one hundred thousand [gold pieces].

Later, on one occasion, while the illustrious Bhoja was gracing the throne, the doorkeeper approached and said: "Your Majesty, a certain poet named Bhavabhūti has arrived from the land of Vārāṇasī and stands at the gate. The king said: "Let him enter. Then he entered and went before the assembly. All the members of the court were delighted by his arrival. Upon seeing Bhavabhūti, the king bowed to him. He, having said "May there be well-being," sat down by the king's command.
Bhavabhūti said: "O Lord, bees are not brought to the honey by means of *pārijāta* flowers; nor are *cakora* birds entreated by the moon to partake of its moonlight.
Yet, these unprecedented manifestations have arrived, sweetened by the sweetness of our own speech."
Let the wise here experience joy spontaneously; what is the use of vain entreaties?

We have no palanquin, nor any ornament such as bracelets or the like; we have no lofty horse, no follower whatsoever, and no beautiful garment. However, [we possess] all those learned men dwelling upon the surface of the earth who delight in the science of literature (sāhityavidyā).
We possess a faultless knowledge that brings satisfaction to the mind and causes the head to bow. 246.
Having heard this, the son of the scholar Bāṇa said: "Ah, you sinner! Do not display such arrogance in the assembly of the Lord of Dhārā.
Not even a breath escapes from the path of Bāṇa’s heart;
how much less can Sarasvatī, bound by feet of manifest ostentation, find its way out? (247)
Then Bhavabhūti, unable to endure this defeat, said:
"Alas! If a man who merely composes a few words forcibly extracted from others were to be considered a rival to a poet whose speech flows with mastery—"
Whether it happens today or tomorrow—what need is there for much talk? In this sinful Kali age, there is a conflict between the maker of pots and the creator of the three worlds.
He spoke again: "The speech of the poet Kālidāsa, even today, if it should ever attain equality with my words, does so only while trembling in fear at every step. (249)
Then Kālidāsa said: "Friend Bhavabhūti, you are a great poet! What more need be said here?
This assembly of King Dhārā, adorned with the greatest scholars, knows the difference between us two—or perhaps only the king, who is like Śiva himself. (250)
Having heard that, the king said: "The conclusion of lovemaking must be described by you both. Bhavabhūti replied:

"The moon's orb has become divested of its ornaments; the sky, with its scattered stars, has appeared like a pearl necklace; the god of love’s bow has lost its vigor as the blue lotuses close their petals."

With its sweet-throated birds hidden away and its humming silenced by the gentle breezes, and with its clusters of blossoms motionless, that campaka creeper became still; I know not what happened thereafter. || 251 ||
Then Kālidāsa said:
"The lunar orb is weary; the darkness, bound by the weight of garlands, is disheveled;
even before this, the smile has played like the tips of blooming kaitaka flowers."
The dancing of the earrings has ceased, the pair of blue lotuses is closed, and the hissing of the coral-like lips has vanished; therefore, I know not what remained thereafter. || 252 ||

The king said to Kālidāsa, “O good poet, you should not speak of equality with Bhavabhūti. Bhavabhūti replied, “Your Majesty, why do you disparage me? The king said, “In every respect, you are a poet. Then Bāṇa said, “O King, if Bhavabhūti is a poet, what need is there to mention Kālidāsa? The king said, “O poet Bāṇa, Kālidāsa is no poet at all.”

"But for Pārvatī, it is surely some incarnation of a man upon this earth. Then Bhavabhūti said, "Your Majesty, what excellence shines forth here? The King replied, "Bhavabhūti, what need is there to speak of the excellence in Kālidāsa’s verse? For he has recited: 'Her smile plays like the filaments of the kaitaka flower. Then Bhavabhūti said, "Your Majesty, you speak out of partiality. Thereupon Kālidāsa said, "Your Majesty, let there be no ill-repute."

"Having gone to the temple of the goddess Bhuvaneśvarī and placing her [the manuscript] before her, you must have it weighed against the jar. Then Bhoja, surrounded by the entire assembly of poets, reached the temple of Bhuvaneśvarī; there, in her presence, he placed the jar into the hand of Bhavabhūti, wrote the two verses on two identical leaves, and set them upon the scale.

Then, perceiving that a slight elevation had arisen in Bhavabhūti’s portion due to his lightness, the Goddess—who is ever dependent on her devotees—thinking "let there be no humiliation of him in this assembly," took the nectar from the jasmine flower in her own ear-ornament with the tip of her left fingernail and cast it onto Bhavabhūti’s leaf. Thereupon Kālidāsa said:
"Oh, what great fortune! My own speech and that of Bhavabhūti, having been placed upon the balance scale, reflect back [in equal measure] within that lightness."
The divine Goddess of Speech immediately casts the sweetness of the pollen from the buds of the *kahlāra* lilies, gathered by her ears, for the sake of perfecting [the poem]. || 253 ||
Thereupon Bhavabhūti fell at the feet of Kālidāsa and regarded the king as a true connoisseur. Then the king gave a hundred rutting elephants to the poet Bhavabhūti.

On another occasion, while wandering alone at night in the city of Dhārā, the king saw a golden courtesan going to a rendezvous; he asked her, "O lady, who are you? Where are you going alone in the middle of the night? Thereupon, that clever courtesan, realizing that it was the illustrious Bhoja wandering at night, said:
"O King, O Lord of the Earth, the god of love (Viṣameṣu) is more formidable even than you."
Rudra and the others carry out his teaching upon their heads like servants. || 254 ||

Thereupon, the king, being pleased, took a bracelet and an armlet from his own arm and gave them to her; she received them at the appropriate places. Then, while traveling on the road, he saw a woman weeping alone in a certain house and sent a bodyguard to investigate, thinking, "For what reason does she weep at midnight? What is her sorrow? Thereafter, the bodyguard returned and said: "O King, listen to what she said when I questioned her:
'My husband is old and lies upon a bedstead; this house remains only as a pillar.'"
This is the season of the monsoon, yet there is no news of my son’s well-being;
seeing her own daughter-in-law, languid from the weight of pregnancy, distressed because the oil-flask—filled with great effort drop by drop—has broken, the mother-in-law weeps for a long time. (255)
Then the king, an ocean of compassion, gave her a hundred thousand [gold pieces].
On another occasion, a Brahmin residing in the Koṅkaṇa country said "Svasti" to the king and spoke:
"O Bhoja, heaven and earth are within the two shells of the oyster of your fame in the ocean."
I believe that the orb of the moon is a pearl produced from that [lake]. (256)
The king gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces].

On another occasion, a certain man from the land of Kashmir, who was nothing more than a loincloth, having seen the poets in the king’s presence adorned with gold, rubies, silk garments, and fine cloths, said to the king:
"There is no sound of excellent bracelets upon my hands, nor are there earrings in my ears."

O King, our garments possess a beauty as pure as milk churned upon trembling shores; our ornament is the brilliance of our teeth; we have neither palanquin nor horse, for they are surpassed by the entire universe. We possess only one thing: skill in the art of eloquent speech within the royal assembly.
Then the king gave him one hundred thousand [gold pieces].
On another occasion, seeing the lunar orb at night, the king described the spot within it:
"Some suspected it to be a deer; others thought it was the mud of the ocean."
"Some said it was a deer, while others claimed it was the shadow of the earth.
Having written this first half-verse, the King placed it in Kālidāsa’s hand. Then, at that very moment, the poet wrote the second half:
"That which appears on the moon, dark as a fragment of polished sapphire—"
We declare that this thick, dense darkness drunk at night is situated within the belly.

The king gave one hundred thousand gold pieces as a reward for the second half of the verse. Then, having observed the style of Kālidāsa’s poetry, the king was filled with wonder and spoke again: "Friend, describe the spotless moon. Thereupon the poet recited:

"It is a pleasure-pond for the goddess Lakṣmī, a white mansion for Rati, a mirror for the maidens of the quarters, a flower for the dark vine of Night, and a parasol for Manmatha, the conqueror of the three worlds."
The moon, a white bull for the sphere of the stars, leads away the massed smile of Hara— a white lotus of the celestial river— and the pool of nectar that is its moonlight.
The king, however, gave him a reward of one hundred thousand coins.
Once, a certain poet of the vīṇā came from a distant land and said:

"I am neither one whose intellect has traveled the paths of logic and grammar, nor am I a knower of literary aesthetics; I do not know that most wonderful skill in the composition of diverse sentences."

Some goddess, the daughter of the beloved of Virañci, holds a lute in her hand; nevertheless, she speaks something indescribable with a voice that breaks my heart, even as it resonates from her mouth. || 260 ||
The king gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Having heard his exquisitely beautiful composition, Bāṇa said:

"O King, those who know the art of sound do not touch this sweetness, as if it were an outcaste woman; and those intoxicated by sentiment do not behold this supreme erudition, as if it were a girl of noble family."
The union of the sweetness of refined expression and the fragrance that is a friend to musk and camphor becomes an elixir for the ears of some fortunate person alone. (261)
On another occasion, the king said to Sītā at dawn: "O Queen, describe the break of day. Sītā replied:
"The stars have become sparse and large, like virtuous men in the final stage of life;
like the mind of a sage, the sky has become serene everywhere."
Darkness departs from the mind, just as a wicked person leaves the virtuous; and night passes away quickly, like prosperity leaves those who lack diligence. || 262 ||
The king, having given a hundred thousand, said to Kālidāsa: "Friend, O excellent poet, you too must describe the dawn. Kālidāsa replied:
"The eastern quarter has become tawny like mercury; behold, the moon has lost its luster like a learned man in an assembly of villagers."
The stars, exhausted by the passing moment, do not shine like kings intent on no exertion; nor do the lamps gleam, like the virtues of those devoid of wealth. || 263 ||
The king gave him a hundred thousand coins for every single syllable.

On another occasion, the gatekeeper approached and said, "Your Majesty, a certain florist’s wife is standing at the gate. The king said, "Let her enter. She was then ushered in; having offered her salutations, she recited:
"With a sweet lute sounding from a gourd-cup kissed by clusters of high, firm breasts; with eyebrows that captivate the world of the gods..."
"Your fame is being sung, as white as the flood of rays from the moon shimmering upon the tip of Śiva’s crown. || 264 ||
The king, thinking, "Oh, what a magnificent trail of footprints! gave her one hundred thousand coins for every single syllable.

On another night, while wandering through the city of Dhārā, the king saw a certain beautiful woman in someone's house intent upon using a mortar. Beholding that young woman with a face like the full moon and delicate limbs, he spoke to the pestle held in her hand: "O pestle, even by the touch of this maiden’s sprout-like hands, you did not become a sprout; therefore, you are nothing but wood in every respect. Then the king recited a verse: "One who possesses a body as delicate as a lotus stalk, Whose face is like the full moon, And whose speech is as sweet as honey— How can such a one be compared to wood? (1) Then the king recited a second verse: "Even though she is as delicate as a lotus stalk, Her feet are marked with the signs of royalty; She is the daughter of a king, Not a mere wooden pestle.
