(16) Then the king recited
"Your *musala* sprout is that which has not yet been born this very moment.

Then, in the morning, seeing Kālidāsa arrived at the assembly hall, the king recited, "Your *musala* sprout is that which has not yet been born this very moment," and said, "O good poet, recite the third line. Thereupon Kālidāsa said:
"It is well known in the world that you are surely indeed wood..."
And yet, it is said to be true that you were raised in the forest;
for at this festival of union with the hands of the girl whose eyes are like fresh blue lotuses, your sprout-like mace has not yet emerged from its sheath.
Thereupon, the king gave one hundred thousand coins for every single syllable of those three verses.

On another occasion, having spent a long time sporting in the water, the king, being exhausted, sat down in the shade of a banyan tree standing on its bank. A certain poet, approaching him there, said:
“O illustrious Bhoja-deva, skilled in protecting the earth, the southern lord of the earth, upon seeing the sky instantly covered by the mass of dust from your army, [cried out]...”
Free from apprehension, free from shame, without followers, without kinsmen, without friends, without women, without offspring, without younger brothers, and without attendants, he departed.

Moreover—The quarters of the sky have been gazed upon by the cranes, whose hearts are filled with joy at an unexpected resolve, and by the flocks of peacocks, who perform sudden and skillful dances; [all these] darkened by the dust raised from the earth by the vast army of yours, which is overflowing with moisture and surging forth. (267)
Then the king gave him two hundred thousand [gold pieces]. At that very moment, seeing a crow cawing on one branch and a cuckoo warbling on another branch, the poet named Devajaya said:

“Neither are your feet beautiful, nor is your beak clever; your speech is not worth mentioning, your gait lacks graceful charm, and this grasp of your wings is not pure. Yet, O cuckoo, you are the one who steals the heart of the world.”
O foolish crow, are you not ashamed to utter here in this place such harsh and screeching cries in vain, while flaunting an unworthy display of "scholarship"? (268)
Then, considering this self-reproach composed by Devajayakavi under the guise of a crow to be directed at him, a poet named Hariśarman, who was his rival, spoke out of anger and envy:
“Accompanied by cuckoos, though black and possessing similar plumage, by whom can a crow be explained unless he speaks for himself? (269)

Then the king, having learned of the mutual enmity between Hariśarman and Devajaya, established friendship between them by having them embrace one another and by bestowing upon them garments, ornaments, and other gifts.

On another occasion, as the king was traveling in a carriage, he saw a certain treasure of asceticism (taponidhi) on the road and said to him: “The sight of those such as you depends upon fortune. Where is your dwelling? And whom do you request for the sake of food? Then, hearing the king’s words, the treasure of asceticism replied:
“Fruit is obtainable at will from the trees in every forest without fatigue;”
At every step, there is cool and sweet water from sacred rivers;
there are beds of soft touch made of delicate sprouts from creepers; yet even so, the wretched stand at the gates of the wealthy, enduring their torment. (270)
"O King, we do not request anything from anyone, nor do we accept gifts. The king, pleased, bowed to him.
Then, a certain man arriving from the northern region said "Svasti" to the king. The king asked him, "Learned one, where is your residence? The learned man replied:
"Where water is reviled as mere nectar, and where outcastes [regard themselves as] lords of the gods."
And the wish-fulfilling gem is but a stone; O Lord, our dwelling is not there. || 271 ||

Then the king, having given a hundred thousand [gold pieces], said: "What is the special news from the land of Kāśī? He replied: "O King, a certain wonderful report has now been heard there from the mouths of the people: 'The gods are distressed with grief. The king asked: 'Learned one, whence comes grief for the gods? And he said:
'Where shall we dwell today? Bhoja has given us the Golden Mountain (Meru).
Thus the minds of the gods are agitated; this is the new report concerning Bhoja. (272)
Then the king, pleased by the man's words of curiosity, gave him another hundred thousand.

Thereupon the gatekeeper said, "Your Majesty, a certain learned scholar devoted to celibacy has arrived from Śrīśaila and stands at the door. The king said, "Let him enter. Then the celibate student approached and said, "May you live long! The king asked him, "O Brahmin, why do you observe such a vow, contrary to the spirit of this Kali age, even in your youth?"

“You have become emaciated by fasting every day; I shall cause the daughter of a certain Brahmin to be given to you, provided that you accept the duties of a householder. The student replied: “O Lord, you are the Sovereign. What is impossible for you?
Deer are my friends, my home is a mountain cave, peace is my beloved wife, my sustenance is wild creepers and fruits, and my clothing is the excellent bark of trees.”

For those whose minds are immersed in the flood of the nectar of that meditation, and who find such bliss [in this world], they have no longing even for liberation, O Lord who bears the crescent moon as your crest-ornament. || 273 ||

The king rose and fell at his feet, saying, "O Brahmin, what must I do? He replied, "Your Majesty, we wish to go to Kāśī; therefore, please act accordingly. Send all those who are the best among scholars in your court, along with their wives, toward Kāśī. Then, satisfied by the company [of such men], I shall go to Kāśī. The king did as he was told. Thereupon, all the eminent scholars set out by his command.

Kālidāsa alone did not go. Then the king said to Kālidāsa, "O good poet, why have you not gone? Thereupon Kālidāsa said to the king: "O Lord, you are omniscient! Those wise men who dwell far from Śambhu go to sacred pilgrimage sites; but he in whose heart Gaurīśvara resides, O King Bhoja, he indeed possesses all holy waters. (274)
Then, after the learned men had departed for Kāśī, the king once asked Kālidāsa in the assembly hall: "Kālidāsa, have you heard anything today? He replied:
"On Mount Meru, in the caves of Mandara, on the slopes of the Himavat, on the mountain of Mahendra, on the rocky surfaces of Kailāsa, and even on the ridges of the Malaya mountains."
O Bhoja, I have heard your fame being sung repeatedly by throngs of celestial bards who traverse the worlds and the horizon, even upon the Sahya mountain. || 275 ||
Thereupon, the king was filled with wonder and granted a hundred thousand coins for every single syllable.

Later, on one occasion, the king, observing that the assembly of scholars had departed and learning that Kālidāsa was incessantly addicted to courtesans, reflected: "Alas! Bāṇa, Mayūra, and the others have carried out my command; yet this man, due to his addiction to courtesans, does not respect my order. What shall we do? Thereafter, the king looked upon Kālidāsa with contempt.

Then, perceiving the King’s contempt for himself, Kālidāsa went to the land of Ballāla; having reached the ruler of that country, he said: "O Lord, I am a poet named Kālidāsa who has come to your realm out of disregard from the King of Mālava, Bhoja. Thereupon, the King seated him upon a throne and said: "O good poet, the greatness of that [Bhoja] has been celebrated here hundreds of times by scholars who have come from his court. O good poet, they say you are Sarasvatī herself. Therefore, recite something. Then Kālidāsa said:
“O King Ballāla, a Kirāta woman wandering through the city of your enemy, having gathered scattered jewels and her limbs agitated by the suspicion that they were glowing coals of vast khadira wood,
threw pieces of sandalwood over them and, blowing upon them with eyes half-closed, [beheld the truth].”
It bears the suspicion of being smoke because of the swarms of bees following the fragrance of its breath.
Thereupon, he gave him one hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every single syllable.
Then, on one occasion, King Vallāla asked Kālidāsa: "O good poet, describe the city of Ekaśilā. Thereupon the poet said:
"In the city of Ekaśilā, the side-glances of the fawn-eyed women are preceded by pretexts..."
"In every street, at every step, young men are being bound in chains without any fault. || 277 ||
And again he gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for each syllable. Furthermore, the poet recites:

"In these ponds, young men are struck by the curved side-glances—like the arrows of the Bodiless One—of those women with eyes as broad as lotus petals, who have come here from lakes as vast as the ocean. (278)
Furthermore, King Ballāla gave a hundred thousand [gold pieces] for every single syllable. Thus Kālidāsa remained right there.

In the meantime, having reached the city of Dhārā, the gatekeeper said to Bhoja: “O Lord, an eminent scholar named Māgha has arrived from the land of Gurjara and is staying outside the city; he has sent his wife to the royal gate. Your Majesty, please have her enter. Then Māgha’s wife was ushered in. She placed a letter in the king’s hand. The king took it and read:
“The grove of night-lotuses is shorn of its beauty, and the glorious cluster of day-lotuses...”
The owl abandons its joy, while the cakravāka bird is filled with delight;
the sun rises, and the moon sets—alas, how strange is the reversal of fortune for those struck down by fate! 279.

Thus it was said. Having heard that wonderful description of the dawn, the king gave three hundred thousand [gold pieces] and said to Māgha’s wife: "Mother, this is given for your sustenance. Tomorrow morning, I shall come to the scholar Māgha, pay my respects, and fulfill his heart's desire. Then, as she was departing taking that wealth, she heard from the mouths of beggars her husband’s virtues, which were as bright as the rays of the autumnal moon; she consequently gave away the entire sum bestowed by Bhoja to those very beggars.

Having approached her husband, Māghapaṇḍita, she said: “Lord, I have been highly honored by King Bhoja; having heard of your virtues, he has given all his wealth to beggars. Māgha replied: “Queen, well done! But these beggars are surely arriving; what is there to give them? Then, perceiving that Māghapaṇḍita had nothing left but his clothes, a certain petitioner said:
“Having comforted the mountain ranges scorched by the heat of the sun, as well as the forests distressed by fierce forest fires, and having filled hundreds of various rivers and streams—”
O cloud, that you are empty is itself your supreme glory.
Having heard this, Māgha said to his wife: "O Queen, there are no riches, yet wicked hope does not leave me;
my wayward mind takes delight in renunciation."
Begging brings about humiliation, and there is sin in killing oneself;
let your life-breaths depart of their own accord—what is the use of lamentation? (281)
The torment of the fire of poverty has been quenched by the water of contentment; but by what can the internal burning caused by the frustration of the hopes of supplicants be extinguished? (282)
Thus it was said. Then, having observed that state of Māgha Paṇḍita, all the beggars departed for their respective places. As those beggars were thus leaving as they pleased, Māgha spoke:
"Go, go! My life-breaths have become useless now that my supplicants have departed. Even later I must depart; where can such wealth as this be found again? (283)
Thus lamenting, the scholar Māgha passed away to the other world. Then, when her husband had gone to the other world, Māgha’s wife said:
“He whose house the kings always served like servants—that very scholar Māgha now dies, accompanied by his own wife. (284)

Then the king, having learned that Māgha had passed away, went there that very night from his own city in silence, accompanied by a hundred Brahmins. Thereupon, seeing the king, Māgha’s wife said: "O King, since this most excellent scholar departed for the next world this morning while in your realm, you must properly perform the remaining rites for him. Then the king, having conveyed Māgha to the bank of the Narmadā, performed the funeral consecration according to the prescribed ritual.

Thereupon, Māgha’s wife entered the fire. Bhoja attended to both of them with every care as if they were his own children. Then, when Māgha had departed for heaven, the king became increasingly overwhelmed by grief; moreover, due to his separation from Kālidāsa and the departure of the other scholars, he grew thinner day by day, like the moon during the dark fortnight. Thereafter, the ministers met together and deliberated: "Kālidāsa resides in the land of Ballāla. When he arrives, the king will find happiness."

Having deliberated thus, the ministers wrote something on a letter, placed that letter in the hand of one minister, and sent him off. In due course, he reached Kālidāsa and, bowing and saying, "I have been sent by the king's ministers," he gave him the letter. Then Kālidāsa read it: "The anger of the virtuous does not last; even if it lasts, it does not fail in its fruit. It is equal to the affection of the base. (285)
O young cuckoo, after staying for a long time with grace upon the mango tree,
are you not ashamed to have abandoned it today and now wandering among other trees?
Just as the beauty of the cuckoo's song is found in the mango tree, consider whether it could be the same in a khadira or a palāśa tree. (287)

Thus it was said. Then, at dawn, Kālidāsa took leave of that king, traveled to the Mālava country, and stayed in the royal pleasure garden. When the king learned that he had arrived there, he went in person with a large retinue, brought him back, and honored him. Subsequently, when the circle of scholars had assembled in due course, that assembly of Bhoja shone as it had before.

Then, as Bhoja was seated upon his throne, a doorkeeper approached, prostrated himself, and said: "O King, a certain scholar has arrived from the land of Jālandhara and stands at the gate. The king replied, "Admit him. That scholar entered the assembly; seeing the king in such a state and the preeminent poets such as Kālidāsa, who were honored by the world, he became as if tongue-tied. Nothing at all emerged from his mouth in that assembly.
Then the king said, "Scholar, recite something. He replied:
Fearing the burning sensation caused by drinking fermented gruel, Sarasvatī has departed from my mouth;
therefore, O Lord whose hands are occupied with grasping the tresses of Lakṣmī, the enemy of Kamsa, I possess no poetic skill.
The king gave him a hundred queens. On another occasion, the king, filled with curiosity, said to Sītā: “O Queen, recite the *Suratam*. Sītā replied:
“Homage to that *Surata* (the act of love), which is the cause of joy for the entire world;
its incidental fruit is [attained] by those like you, O King Bhoja. (289)
Thereupon, the king, being pleased, gave her a necklace.
Then, looking at the courtesan who was holding the fly-whisk, the king said to Kālidāsa: “O good poet, describe this courtesan. Having observed her, Kālidāsa said:
“From the weight of her hair, the weight of her breasts suffers; from the weight of her breasts, the weight of her hair fears [to suffer].”
O moon-faced one, what is this marvel regarding the hips that bear the weight of the breasts? 290.
Bhoja, being pleased, recited himself:
"From her face come this pair of feet; from her speech come her lower lip and the row of teeth;
from her shimmering [hair] come this pair of breasts; yet the pair of eyes does not tremble from the waist. (291)

Once, while wandering alone through the city of Dhārā, King Bhoja went to the house of a certain eminent brahmin and saw there a golden image of a devoted wife lying on her lap, supporting her husband. Then, the child, having awakened from sleep, moved toward a flame. This woman, who was solely devoted to the duty of a wife, did not wake her husband; nor did she catch the child as he fell into the fire. Witnessing this marvel, the king stood still.

Then she, devoted solely to her duty toward her husband, prayed to Vaiśvānara: "O Lord of Sacrifice! You are the witness of all actions and you know all dharmas. You know me to be dependent on my duty to my husband and not having taken hold of my child. Therefore, having shown favor to my child, do not burn me. Thereupon, the child entered the Lord of Sacrifice, took him by the hand, and remained right there for the duration of half a ghaṭikā.

Thereupon the child ceased weeping and his face became serene, while she remained absorbed in meditation. Then, when her husband happened to rise up, she suddenly took up the child. Beholding that supreme Dharma, the king was overcome with wonder and said: "Aha! Who possesses fortune equal to mine, that such meritorious women as these dwell even in my city?"

Then, having arrived at the assembly hall in the morning and seated upon the lion-throne, the king said to Kālidāsa: “O good poet, a great marvel was seen by me last night. Having said this, the king recited: “The fire is cool as sandalwood paste. Thereupon, Kālidāsa immediately recited the remaining three lines: “Seeing her son falling into the fire, the devoted wife did not awaken her husband. Then, due to the weight of her devotion to her husband, the fire became cool as sandalwood paste. (292)
The king, perceiving his intention, was struck with wonder; he embraced him and fell at his feet.

Once, during the summer season, while the king was wandering through the inner apartments, tormented by the heat of the sun, he experienced the service of affectionate conversation and other courtesies along with those women who were not performing embraces and such acts; having fallen asleep right there, the king rose in the morning and entered the assembly hall, where, out of curiosity, he recited:
“Even at a time when one is wide awake, [the world] remains utterly empty of news of the arrival of the wind.”
Bhavabhūti says:
"The female serpent directed her own hiss toward her hungry offspring with the breath of her mouth;
even at a time when there was news of the arrival of the wind, she remained fully awake and fully aroused. (293)
The king said, "Bhavabhūti, you have spoken the popular proverb correctly. Then, with a sidelong glance, the king looked at Kālidāsa. Thereupon he said:
"Amidst women, the playful lovers experienced fresh embraces even with their eyes alone;
yet when the time was empty even of news of the arrival of the breeze, [the longing] remained fully awakened and increased. (294)
Then the king, having understood his intention, was pleased and honored Kālidāsa with special distinction.

On another occasion, the king, overcome by his passion for hunting and being extremely exhausted, sat down at the foot of a jambu tree with dense shade on the shore of a certain lake. While the king was lying there, many monkeys shook all the jambu fruits from above the tree. Seeing them fall with a loud noise, the king remained for a moment to relieve his fatigue; then, rising and mounting his excellent horse, he departed.

Then, in the assembly, the king, imitating the sound of fruit falling when shaken by a monkey as he had previously experienced it, posed the poetic challenge (samasyā): “*gulugugguluguggulu*. Thereupon Kālidāsa said:
“Ripe *jambū* fruits fall into the clear water;
from the branches shaken by monkeys, *gulugugguluguggulu*. (295)
The king, being pleased, said: "O good poet, how do you know even the unperceived heart of another! You are indeed Śāradā herself! Thus he spoke, falling again and again at his feet.

Once, while wandering in the city of Dhārā in disguise, the king went to the house of a certain elderly brāhmaṇa at midday and remained there. At that time, having performed the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and taking the food offering for the crows (*kākabali*), the old brāhmaṇa went outside the house, placed it on the ground purified with water, and called out to the crow. Thereupon, by the flapping of his hands and the cry of "Hā-hā!", the crows arrived; among them, one crow shrieked loudly.

Hearing that, his young wife, as if terrified, placed her hand upon her breast and cried out, "O Mother! Then the Brahmin said, "My dear one of virtuous character, why are you afraid? She replied, "Lord! For women like me who are devoted to their husbands, the hearing of such a cruel sound is unbearable. The Brahmin said, "Virtuous one, let it be so."

Then the king, having observed all her conduct, reflected: "Aha! This young woman is surely of ill character, since she fears [her husband] so sincerely and herself proclaims her own devotion to him. Surely this fearless woman must be performing some extremely cruel deed at night. Having thus resolved, the king remained right there, invisible during that very night.

Then, at midnight, while her husband was asleep, she had a basket of meat carried by the hand of a courtesan and went to the bank of the Narmadā. The king also followed her, concealing himself. Having reached the Narmadā, she gave the meat to the crocodiles that had gathered there, crossed the river, and dallied with her beloved, who was impaled on the tip of a stake on the opposite bank.
Having witnessed that conduct, the king returned home; in the morning, seeing Kālidāsa in the assembly hall, he said: "O good poet, listen:
'Afraid of the cawing of crows during the day...'"
Then Kālidāsa said: "He crosses the Narmadā at night.
Thereupon, the king was pleased and spoke again:
"In that water there are crocodiles";
therefore, the wise man said: "That very Sundarī knows my vital spots. (296)
Then the king fell at the feet of Kālidāsa.

Once, while wandering through the city of Dhārā, the king saw a certain beautiful woman on the street of courtesans, intent on playing with a ball; as she moved, the speed of her spinning caused her ear-ornament to fall at his feet. Seeing this, he said in the assembly, “Let the poets describe the ball. Then Bhavabhūti said:
“O Ball, your heart is surely known [to me], as if greedy for union with the lips of a young woman!”
Struck by the lotus-hands of women, you fall again and again, yet you rise once more.
Then Vararuci said:
"Though it is but one, this ball appears as if threefold, dyed a deep red by the glow of my beloved’s palm."
Upon the ground, he appeared exceedingly white with the rays of light from his toenails, while remaining composed, he was intensely blue with the rays of his eyes. || 298 ||
Then Kālidāsa said: "The ball, assuming the form of her breast, was indeed struck repeatedly with her hand in anger;
as if terrified by the shape of her eyes, the blue lotus fell at the woman's feet to seek her favor. (299)

Then the king, being pleased, gave a hundred thousand coins (*lakṣa*) to each of the three; however, he especially honored Kālidāsa, who had understood the meaning of the unseen flower that had fallen as an ornament.

Later, on one occasion, while the king was intent on viewing works of art, he saw a painted Great Śeṣa and remarked, "It is well-drawn. Then a certain poet named Śivaśarman praised the king under the guise of praising Śeṣa:
"There are many hooded serpents who are intent on devouring frogs..."
For he alone remains as the sole one capable of supporting the earth.

Then the king, having understood his intention, gave him a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Once, when the winter season had arrived, while attending upon the blazing Hasantī, the king said to Kālidāsa: "O good poet, describe Hasantī. Thereupon the good poet said:
"Like the intellect of a poet, she is full of brilliance; like the hour of dawn, her wheels are well-fashioned;
like the form of Hara, she shines as Hasantī, endowed with smokeless fire. (301)
The king gave him one hundred thousand gold coins.

Once, while in his inner apartments, King Bhoja beheld four of his own wives who were worthy of enjoyment and possessed equal virtues. Among them, he observed these four qualities: Padmāvatī, the daughter of the Lord of Kuntala, had her menstrual bath; Candramukhī, the daughter of the King of Aṅga, had reached her fertile period by natural succession; Kamalā had obtained access through a victory won at dice as a wager; and Līlādevī, the chief queen, had sent for him under the pretext of dispatching a female messenger. Having thus seen these four qualities, the king reflected upon the relative deficiency or excellence among those very qualities.

In all those matters, the king of kings, the illustrious Bhoja—a treasure-house of courtesy—reflected with equanimity for the duration of two or three *ghaṭikās*; then, unable to determine any particular distinction, he fell asleep. Rising in the morning and having performed his daily rites, he went to the assembly hall.

There, while seated upon his throne, King Bhoja beheld Kālidāsa—the ornament of the entire circle of learned men and poets—and said, "O good poet, hear this verse with its third and fourth quarters missing as a poetic puzzle (*samasyā*). Having spoken thus, he recited: "Two or three *nāḍikās* passed while my mind was bewildered by indecision. Having recited this, the king said to Kālidāsa, "O good poet, complete this verse."

Then Kālidāsa, perceiving his heart as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of his hand, recited that verse-fragment (*samasyā*) distinguished by three feet each consisting of more than three syllables: "O King, the daughter of the Lord of Kuntala stands having bathed; today is the turn of the Queen of Aṅga; this night was won at dice by Kamalā; now the Queen must be propitiated.
While the King was contemplating these qualities of the women of the inner apartments—each superior to the last—his mind became bewildered by indecision, and two or three *nāḍikās* passed.
Then the king fell at the feet of Kālidāsa, who had indeed known his own heart; and the circle of poets was filled with wonder.

Once, while wandering through the city of Dhārā, the king saw a certain woman with a face like the full moon approaching, carrying a full water-pot. Hearing a certain sound from the water in that pot, he thought, "Surely, when she embraces her neck, this jar is cooing like the warbling of love-making," and said to Kālidāsa in the assembly: "The cooing is the cooing of love. The poet replied: *ratikūjitamiva kūjitaṃ kalaṃ jalabhṛtastava kumbhasya | śrutvā na yasya hṛdaye dayitā-dhṛtaghaṭā kiṃ sa paṇḍito nāma?* "Is he not truly a scholar whose heart does not break upon hearing the sweet cooing of your water-filled jar, which sounds like the warbling of love?"*
When the woman is clever, with a beautiful face and flushed cheeks, seated upon the hips, and her neck embraced by her lover, that cooing is called the "cooing of love" (ratikūjita). || 303 ||
Then the king, being pleased, gave him a reward of one hundred thousand [gold pieces] in person and bowed to him.

Once, in a great pool in the Narmadā, a certain fragment of stone was seen with some slightly blurred characters upon it. They reflected, "Something here appears as if written; surely this must be brought into the presence of the King. With this thought, they brought it to the court of Bhoja. Hearing of it, Bhoja said: "It is heard that formerly the venerable Hanumān composed the glorious Rāmāyaṇa and cast it into this pool."

"Therefore, one must certainly investigate what this is that has been written; thus, the knowledge of scripts must be acquired. Having discerned the characters through the test of lac, he read them. There, a pair of verses was obtained in their proper sequence: "Alas! Indeed, the ripening of past deeds for living beings is truly uneven.
Then Bhoja said, "Let the first half of this be told. At that time, Bhavabhūti replied:
Where indeed is the stainless lineage of this long-eyed woman, and where is this scandal of association with a night-stalker?
Alas, truly incongruous is the fruit of deeds performed in the past!
For indeed, among living beings, there is the ripening of karmas. || 304 ||
Then Bhoja, considering that there was a flaw in the sound of the verse, recited that same first half-verse differently:
“Where is the daughter of Janaka? Where is the wife of Rāma? And where is this dwelling in the palace of the ten-necked one?
Alas! Indeed, the ripening of past deeds for living beings is truly uneven.”
Then Bhoja said to Kālidāsa: "O good poet, you too recite the heart of a poet. He replied:
"Those heads which once shone upon the head of Śiva—Śiva, Śiva!—now roll at the feet of vultures.
Alas, the ripening of past deeds indeed becomes most cruel for living beings. (306)
Then, having seen that very same verse recited by Kālidāsa on the front surface of that stone slab through the process of clearing away the lac, the king was greatly delighted.

Once, Bhoja had a new palace constructed for his pleasure. Before anyone entered that palace, a certain *brahmarākṣasa* had already taken possession of it. During the night, he would devour those who lived there. Consequently, the king summoned sorcerers and strove to expel him; however, even as they approached, he would devour the sorcerers themselves. Moreover, he remained there reciting only poetry and such works that he had previously mastered. This being the case, the king wondered: "How can this [demon] be removed?"

Thus he reflected. Then Kālidāsa said: "Your Majesty, this Rākṣasa certainly appears to be proficient in all the sciences and a skilled poet. Therefore, I shall accomplish my purpose by pleasing him alone. Let the exorcists stay; behold my mantra. Having said this, he went there himself that night and lay down.

During the first watch of the night, a Brahmarākṣasa arrived. Seeing an unprecedented man, he recited one riddle—a Pāṇinian sūtra—at every watch. Because the answer, which was in his heart, had not been spoken, he would decide, "This man is not a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, he must be killed," and kill him. At that time as well, this man was as unprecedented as before. Therefore, [the king thought], "I must recite the riddle. If he does not give a fitting answer to it, then he must be killed. With this resolve, he recited: *sarvasya dve*. Then Kālidāsa said:
"Good and bad thoughts are the causes for the attainment of excellence and downfall.
Then he departed. Again, returning during the second watch of the night, he recited: "The old man with the youth..."
Thus [it was said]. Then the poet says:
"They are abandoned by amorous women through familiarity.
In the third watch, that *rākṣasa* returned once more and recited:
"Regarding the phrase 'one [is sufficient] for the lineage,' the poet then says:
'He is a man who prevails who supports his family.'"
Thus it was said. Then, having arrived during the fourth watch of the night, that Rākṣasa recited:
“A woman [is treated] like a man.
Thereupon, the poet said:
"For when that [virtue] prevails, the household is truly destroyed. || 307 ||

Thus it was said. Then that Rākṣasa, having understood his own intention even during the four watches of the night, was pleased; at the time of dawn he arrived, embraced him, and said: "O wise one, I am pleased. What is your desire? Kālidāsa replied: "Venerable sir, we must leave this house and go elsewhere. He too, saying "So be it," departed. Thereafter, the delighted Bhoja honored the poet greatly.

Once, while the illustrious Bhoja, the crest-jewel of all monarchs, was presiding upon his throne, the doorkeeper approached and said: “Your Majesty, a certain poet named Mallinātha from the Deccan, possessing nothing but a loincloth, stands at the gate. The King said, “Let him enter. Then the poet arrived, uttered the word “May it be well,” and having sat down by the King’s command, he recited: “The elephant shines with rut; the sky with clouds; the night with the full moon;
a woman with character; a horse with speed; and a palace with constant festivities.”
Speech is [glorified] by grammar, rivers by pairs of swans, an assembly by scholars, a lineage by a virtuous son, the earth by you, and the three worlds by the sun. || 308 ||
Then the king said, "O learned one, what is your purpose? Thereupon the poet replied:
"The mother is angry with neither me nor my daughter-in-law; she too is angry with neither me nor her daughter-in-law. I am angry with neither her nor her. Tell me, O King, whose fault is this? (309)
Thus, the king, having recognized the fault of poverty, fulfilled the poet's desire.

Once, the gatekeeper approached and said to the king, "Your Majesty, a great poet named Kaviśekhara stands at the door. The king said, "Let him enter. Then the poet, having arrived and said "Greetings," recited:
"O King, I have received a refusal from the gatekeeper himself."
"O Lord of the Earth, I desire from you a rutting elephant."

Then the king, standing facing the east and exceedingly delighted, thinking that the entire eastern region had been given to the poet, turned toward the south. Thereupon the poet thought, "What is this? The king has turned his face away and does not look at me. Then, having arrived in the southern region and facing him, the poet recited: "This is an unprecedented science of archery taught by you; how is it that the flood of arrows comes forth while the string goes to the ends of the quarters? (311)
Then the king, having mentally given even the southern region to the poet, turned himself toward the west. The poet, arriving there, said:
“This world speaks falsely of you as being omniscient; you do not know how to utter even a single word when a beggar says, ‘There is nothing. (312)
Then the king, thinking that this region too had been given away by Kavi, turned his face toward the north. Kavi, having arrived there as well, said:
“It is falsely said by the wise that you are always a giver of everything;
for enemies have never gained your back, nor have the wives of others gained your chest. (313)
Then the king, thinking that the land had been given by Kavi, rose up. And Kavi, not understanding his intention, spoke again:
"O King, while you rain down showers of gold everywhere, not even a single drop falls upon me, who am covered by the umbrella of misfortune. (314)

Then the king, having gone to the inner apartments, said to Queen Līlā: “O Queen, the entire kingdom has been given to the poet; therefore, come with me to the forest of asceticism. At that moment, the learned man came out to the door. He was asked by the elderly minister Buddhisāgara: “Learned one, what was given by the king? He replied: “Nothing at all. Then the minister said: “Recite the verse spoken there. Thereupon, the poet recited four verses.

Then the minister said, “O good poet, ten million pieces of wealth are given to you; however, whatever has been given to you here by the king, sell that back. The poet did so. Then, having given the ten million pieces of wealth and sent the poet away, the minister returned and stood before the king. At that time, the king said to him, “Buddhisāgara, this entire kingdom is given to the poet. I shall go to the forest of asceticism along with my wives.”

"In that penance grove, if you have any regard for me, come along with me. Then the minister said, "Your Majesty, this kingdom has been sold by that poet for the price of ten million pieces of gold, and those ten million pieces of gold have been given to the learned man; therefore, the kingdom is yours alone. Enjoy it. At that, the king honored Buddhisāgara with special distinction.

On another occasion, while the king was wandering through the forest in his passion for hunting, his body withered by the sun burning upon his forehead, he became overwhelmed by thirst. Mounting his horse in search of water, he wandered along the nearby bank; finding none, he grew exhausted and sat down beneath a certain great tree. There, a certain cowherd girl—possessing all limbs that were delicate and beautiful—arrived by chance, carrying a vessel of buttermilk, intending to sell it in the city of Dhārā.

Seeing her approaching, the king, driven by thirst and with the thought, "If I drink this beverage contained in the vessel, I shall be refreshed," asked, "Young woman, what are you carrying? She, perceiving the Bhoja king from the splendor of his face and sensing his thirst, spoke in the form of a verse under the influence of gazing upon his countenance: "O King of kings, drink this which has the luster of snow, jasmine, the moon, and a conch shell; which possesses the fragrant flavor of a ripe kapittha fruit; which is churned by the sprout-like hands of young women; and which removes all ailments. (315)

Thus it was said. Having drunk that buttermilk, the king was pleased and said to her, “O fair-browed one, what is your desire? She, whose youth was slightly revealed and whose eyes were clouded by the delusion of being overcome by passion, replied, “My Lord, consider me still a maiden. She spoke again:
“As the night-lily to the moon, as the flock of *kokas* to the sun, as the swarm of *cātaka* birds to the cloud, and as the line of bees to the cluster of flowers;”
"O best of kings, just as the beautiful female cuckoo longs for the mango tree, so does this mental state of mine always yearn to behold you, my lord, who have gone abroad. || 316 ||

The king, filled with wonder, said, “Sukumārī, with the consent of Queen Līlā, we accept you. Having thus brought her to the city of Dhārā, he accepted her accordingly. Once, during the royal consecration ceremony, the golden pitcher slipped from the palm of Madirākṣī—who was tormented by the arrows of Love—and fell with a ringing sound upon the steps of the staircase. Then the king, having entered the assembly hall, said to Kālidāsa, “O good poet, complete this poetic puzzle (samasyā): ‘ṭaṭaṃṭaṭaṃṭaṃṭaṭaṭaṃṭaṭaṃṭam. Thereupon Kālidāsa replied:
During the royal consecration, the golden pitcher slipped from the hand of a young woman who was reeling with intoxication;
as it fell along the path of the stairs, it produced the sound: *ṭaṭaṃ-ṭaṭaṃ-ṭaṭaṃ-ṭaṭaṃ-ṭaṭaṃ-ṭaṭaṃ-ṭaṭaṃ-ṭam*.
Then the king, having understood his intention, gave him one hundred thousand gold pieces (*akṣara-lakṣa*).

On another occasion, while the illustrious Bhoja was gracing the throne, a certain thief was brought before the king by the guards. Seeing him, the king asked, "Who is this? Then the guard said, "Your Majesty, by this *kumbhillaka* (thief), goods were stolen through a breach in the wall at a certain prostitute's house. Then the king said, "This man must be punished. Thereupon, a thief named Bhukkuṇḍa said:
“Bhaṭṭi is lost, Bhāravi is lost, the monk is lost, and even Bhīmasena is lost!
I am Bhukkuṇḍa, and you, O King, are the lord of the earth; for Antaka (Death) is stationed within the row of *bhab* sounds.
Then the king said: “O Bhukkuṇḍa, go, go; wander as you please!”

Once, while wandering in the forest exhausted from hunting, King Bhoja, his heart seeking rest, reached a certain lake and remained there, falling asleep from fatigue. Then, when the sun had entered the cavity of the western ocean, night appeared right there, bestowing happiness upon that king—
a night that was like a sprouting shoot of the mass of bliss brought by the shimmering rays of the moon.

Then, at the time of dawn, as the king set out toward the city, he observed the orb of the moon hanging over the slope of the western mountain. Full of curiosity, he returned to the assembly hall, and upon looking at the eminent poets standing nearby, he proposed a poetic fragment (*samasyā*): “The lunar orb hangs upon the slope of the western mountain. Thereupon Bhavabhūti said:
“The stars have departed from the sky due to the masses of the sun’s reddish rays.
Then Daṇḍin said:
"At dawn, it stirs very gently in the cool breeze.
Then Kālidāsa said:
"The orb of the moon clung to the slope of the western mountain, amidst the multitude of young women whose lips were no longer held by their lords."

Then the king honored everyone, and he especially honored Kālidāsa. Now, once upon a time, Bhoja went outside the city and performed the cleansing of his skull with the fresh water of a pond, as he had done since childhood. Because of that, a young fish entered the skull and, having become entangled near the protruding cranium, emerged. Then the king returned to his own city. From that time forward, a pain arose in the king’s skull; though treated thoroughly by the best physicians there, it was not relieved.

Thus, day and night, while the kingdom was utterly unwell due to a great disease unknown to humans, his body became increasingly emaciated and its natural ease departed; his face lost its luster like a lotus in the winter season, resembling the orb of the moon eclipsed by the mouth of Rāhu. His mind turned away from the duties of state, just as a eunuch’s interest turns away from women; the disease grew ever more intense, like a fire in a dry forest.

Thus, even after a year had passed, that disease was not cured by anyone. Consequently, King Bhoja, his mind distressed by the suffering of the illness caused by the consumption of various kinds of medicines, addressed these words with some difficulty to Buddhisāgara—who stood nearby, submerged in an ocean of grief—using distinct syllables: "Buddhisāgara, from now on let no excellent physician whatsoever take up residence within my realm. Cast all the medical treatises of Vāgbhaṭa and others into the river and depart."
"The time for my assembly with the gods has arrived. Upon hearing this, all the citizens, the poets, and the courtiers of the inner harem became bathed in a torrent of falling tears.

Then, on one occasion, in the assembly of the gods, Purandara, seated in the midst of the entire host of sages, said to the sage Vīṇāmuni: “O sage, what is the news now in the world of mortals? Thereupon Nārada replied: “Lord of the gods, there is nothing particularly wonderful. However, the illustrious King Bhoja, a resident of Dhārānagara, is afflicted by disease and remains extremely unwell. No one has been able to cure his illness; consequently, this King Bhoja has even driven the most eminent physicians out of his own country.”

"Thus, it is refuted that even the science of medicine is false. Having heard this, Indra said to the two Nāsatyas standing nearby: "O physicians of heaven, how can the treatise of Dhanvantari be false? Then the two of them replied: 'O Lord, Sovereign of the Immortals, this scripture is not deceptive; however, that Bhoja is not afflicted by a disease unknown to the gods. Indra asked: 'What is this incurable disease known to you two?'"

Then the two of them said, "Your Majesty, Bhoja performed the purification of the skull; at that time, a *pāṭhīna* fish entered it. This disease has its root in that. Thereupon Indra, with a smiling face, said, "Therefore, you two must depart this very moment. Otherwise, from now on, there will be a failure of the science of medicine in the world of mortals. He is indeed the abode of Sarasvatī’s grace and the restorer of the scriptures."

Then, by the command of the Lord of the Gods, both of them, having assumed the guise of Brahmins, reached the city of Dhārā and spoke to the gatekeeper: "Gatekeeper, we are two physicians who have come from the land of Kāśī; inform the illustrious Bhoja that we have arrived. Having heard that he has accepted the medical science as being false, we have come for its re-establishment and for the curing of his disease. Thereupon the gatekeeper said: "O Brahmins, the King has declared that no eminent physician is to be admitted."

"The king, however, is merely unwell; this is not the occasion for a formal petition. At that moment, Buddhisāgara, having gone outside on business, saw them and asked, "Who are you? Thereupon, they told him how they had come. Then Buddhisāgara led them into the presence of the king. When the king beheld them, he perceived from the splendor of their faces that they were human beings; concluding that "this illness can be cured by these two," he honored them greatly.
Then the two said: "O King, do not fear; the disease has departed. However, you must remain in some secluded place. Thereupon, the king did exactly as he was told.

Then those two, having deluded the king with a powder of enchantment, took his skull-cup and the swarm of small fish contained within its cavity; they placed them in a certain vessel, restored the skull to its proper form using the *saṃdhānakaraṇī* (reunion-recipe), and brought him back to life with the *saṃjīvanī* (revivifying-recipe). They then showed it to him. Upon seeing this, the king was struck with wonder and asked them, "What is this?"

Then the two of them said, “O King, this has been obtained by you through the purification of skulls practiced since childhood. Thereupon, the king, recognizing them as the Aśvins, asked for the purpose of that purification, “What is wholesome for us? Then the two of them replied:
“Bathing in water that is not cold, drinking milk, and excellent women [are wholesome].”

"This is the path for you, O humans! In that interval, hearing the address "O humans" in the midst of the assembly, the king thought, "If we are humans, who are you two? and instantly seized their hands with his own hands. Then, at that very moment, the two vanished while saying, "The fourth quarter must be completed by Kālidāsa. Thereupon, the king was struck with wonder and summoned everyone to tell them what had occurred. Upon hearing this, they were all filled with amazement and astonishment. Then, the fourth quarter was completed by Kālidāsa.
“Food that is unctuous and warm. || 322 ||

Thus it was said. Then King Bhoja, regarding Kālidāsa as a playful incarnation of a divine being, honored him most highly. Thereafter, King Bhoja, the lord of Dhārā, increased day by day in strength and splendor, like the moon during its waxing fortnight. Then, on one occasion, while the illustrious Bhoja was gracing the throne and his court was adorned by a multitude of ornaments among the jewels of poets—namely Kālidāsa, Bhavabhūti, Daṇḍin, Bāṇa, Mayūra, Vararuci, and others—the doorkeeper approached and said: "Your Majesty, a certain poet stands at the gate."
"Therefore, let this letter, supported by these verses, be deposited in the assembly hall of the gods. Thus he showed it to him. The king took it and read it:
"A certain young woman, sending [a message] to her lover's dwelling, wrote a seal upon a basket with lac from the hand of a maidservant, which was placed on top of it."
Here, the noble Mallinātha, the lord of poets and expert Tilaka, inquires after the state of Gaurī’s beloved, the son of the Wind, and the Campaka tree. || 323 ||

Upon hearing this, the entire assembly of scholars was filled with wonder. Then Kālidāsa said, “O King, Mallinātha must be summoned immediately. Thereupon, by the king’s command, the gatekeeper ushered the poet in. Having addressed the king with “May it be well,” the poet sat down at his command. Then the king said to that lord of poets, “O learned poet Mallinātha, this verse has been well composed. At that, Kālidāsa replied, “Why say it is ‘well’? It is as if the moon were to praise its own radiance.”

“You are especially praiseworthy for describing the virtuous conduct of your beloved who has gone to another land, particularly through your description that rivals her various emotions. Then Bhavabhūti said, “This verse is distinguished by its description of Hanumān, the son of the Wind, the enemy of the grove of Pampā’s throat. Thereupon, the delighted king gave him a hundred thousand gold pieces, and five elephants and ten horses were bestowed. Then the pleased scholar praised the king:
“O Lord Bhoja, I suspect that this very night has been turned into day by the floods of your water-like gifts.”
Otherwise, how could such a gift be given to stones, cows, and trees as proclaimed by him? (324)
Then, having heard that verse which transcended the worldly, the king once again gave him three hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Thereupon, the treasurer wrote upon the record of merit:

"The illustrious King Bhoja, being pleased after hearing in the assembly this verse of hidden jesting by one separated from his beloved, bestowed ten lakhs of gold, ten excellent horses, and five elephants."
Afterwards, his heart filled with joy from hearing the excellent description of the virtues of that very act of giving,
he bestowed upon that Mallinātha one hundred thousand, another hundred thousand, and yet again another hundred thousand [gold pieces].

Then, on one occasion, King Bhoja said to Kālidāsa: "O good poet, recite our latest composition for me. Thereupon, Kālidāsa, becoming enraged and censuring the king, abandoned that region in an instant and reached the city of Ekaśilā together with Vilāsavatī. Subsequently, overwhelmed with grief due to his separation from Kālidāsa, the king assumed the guise of a Kāpālika and eventually arrived at the city of Ekaśilā in search of him.

Then Kālidāsa, having seen the yogin, questioned him with gentle words: "Yogin, where is your dwelling? The yogin replied, "O good poet, our residence is in the city of Dhārā. Then the poet asked, "Is Bhoja well there? Thereupon the yogin said, "What should I say? The poet then said, "If there is any extraordinary news there, tell it truly."

Then the yogi said, "Bhoja has gone to heaven. Thereupon, the poet fell to the ground and lamented: "O Lord, without you we cannot remain on this earth for even a moment; therefore, I am coming to your side. Having thus lamented profusely, Kālidāsa composed his final verse: "Today Dhārā is without support; Sarasvatī is left without a foundation;
all scholars are shattered, now that King Bhoja has gone to heaven. (326)

Thus, as soon as the poet had uttered the final verse, that yogin fell unconscious upon the ground. Then Kālidāsa, seeing him in such a state, concluded, “This is indeed Bhoja,” and said, “Alas, Great King, I have been deceived by your majesty! Having spoken thus, he immediately recited that verse in a different manner:
“Today Dhārā has its eternal support; Sarasvatī has her constant refuge.
All scholars are truly adorned now that King Bhoja has gone to the earth. (327)
Then Bhoja, having embraced and bowed to him, departed for the city of Dhārā.
At that moment, Muñja’s heart— immovable as a mountain—
plunged into the ocean of the nectar-stream of accumulated joy while Bhoja was still alive.

While the king was intent on performing austerities along with virtuous women, he suddenly abandoned his hair in the Muñja grass, relinquished the burden of sovereignty, and partook in renunciations rather than enjoyments. || 328 ||
The narrative of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Bhojarāja, the sovereign of the city of Dhārā, has reached its conclusion.
